WAR EXPENDITURES-CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: That the first report of the special committee on war expenditures, presented to the house on Monday, July 19, be concurred in.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: WAR EXPENDITURES-CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I realize that this motion requires the unanimous consent of the house, by reason of the fact that the necessary time has not elapsed. However, I wish to facilitate the passing of the motion and therefore I do not raise any objection on that score. I would call the attention of the hon. member who has moved the motion to its phraseology as recorded in Votes and Proceedings No. 114, which we have received this morning. There is in paragraph 3 a typographical error which should not pass the house: "to acquaint subcommittees." I presume this is meant to be " to appoint subcommittees."
Paragraph 4 of the report reads:
To employ such secretarial, reportorial, clerical and other assistance as it may deem necessary.
I take it this is similar to the wording of previous reports of the committee in former sessions. I suggest that the committee ought to consider, in a subsequent report before the house rises, whether the question of assistance, which was mentioned while the debate on the constitution of the war expenditures committee was in progress - I refer to legal assistance, assistance in the way of accountancy, and other expert assistance-should not come within the purview of what is described as "other assistance" in this particular paragraph. It was pointed out by members of the committee that one of the difficulties experienced by those who were attempting to investigate various accounts was that they were handicapped through lack of that type of expert assistance, which they felt was essential if they were to make a proper inquiry into the matters which came before them.
Paragraph 5 of the report reads:
In cases where considerations of national security preclude the publishing of certain

recommendations and of the arguments upon which they are based. . . .
I take it that this is "evidence" rather than argument, but I leave it to those who drafted the motion to see whether or not they require that change to be made in order to carry out their wishes in that regard.
I take it also that paragraph 5 follows the report which has been made by a similar committee in the United Kingdom. I am hoping that the matter of national security will not be taken by the committee or by the house as meaning that we are to have, during the sittings of this committee, a maintenance of that secrecy to which such objection was taken during the debate. With these observations I am quite content that the motion pass.

speechtext: Motion agreed to.

BY-ELECTION IN CARTIER-ALLEGED IRREGULARITIES     MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 31 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, grave irregularities in connection with the compiling of voters lists in the Cartier division of Montreal where a by-election is to be held on August 9, 1943, nomination day being August 2, 1943, and where hundreds of names of non-existent persons have been placed on the lists, some of which irregularities have been admitted publicly by one Lazarus Bavitch, returning officer for the electoral district of Cartier. If I am given leave, Mr. Speaker, to introduce this motion, I have the necessary proofs on my desk.
And leave having been granted:

subtopic: BY-ELECTION IN CARTIER-ALLEGED IRREGULARITIES     MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I would not have introduced this matter at this time in the closing days of the session did I not believe it is a matter of urgent public importance, and I do so to facilitate the conduct of the business of the house because otherwise it would have been necessary to move a motion on going into supply, and that might have delayed the business of the house indefinitely.
The preliminary voters lists were made available to the public only last Thursday. Hence the checking of the lists has been done on a relatively small number of polls, fifteen in all. The addresses of persons who, I shall contend in a moment are either non-existent, improperly on the list or their address not that given on the list, were picked at

Dominion Elections
random and only a small part of each of the fifteen polls was therefore checked. There are 112 polls altogether in the division, and the findings which I shall present to the house in a few moments are illustrative rather than exhaustive. There is no reason to doubt and every reason to believe that the information which I have is merely representative and that the same story could be unfolded as to every one of the polls; all therefore should be investigated.
Altogether some 2,000 names have been checked since last Thursday, checked carefully by persons who are reliable and are in some instances supporting their checkings by affidavits which I have on the desk beside me. Out of some 2,000 names, 650-I repeat, 650- were found to be false or improperly on the list, a proportion of approximately one third.
I said I had some of the affidavits. Not all the checkers were available in the short time at the disposal of those who gave me this information to supply me with affidavits covering all these names, but I am reliably informed and therefore believe that the information I have just given is correct.
The following are among the more striking and in some respects perhaps the more ludicrous findings about which it is worth while to inform the house. For example, a baby seven weeks old listed as a bookkeeper; a little girl five years of age listed as a retired spinster, whatever that may be; a number of non-existent addresses which would make the voter reside over a railway or street intersection; seven voters listed at a United Cigar store; seven voters listed for the store which is now the Liberal candidate's committee room; eleven voters listed in a barber shop; six voters listed at a restaurant. The waiter at the restaurant laughingly told the person who made the inquiry that the enumerator took the names of the persons sitting at the counter.
There are also names of persons who are dead, persons who have moved away for more than a year, fictitious names, fictitious addresses, and the names of persons who are not citizens of Canada. The most common occurrence was the enumeration of an entire family without any regard to age. Indeed it seems as though the enumerators in the Cartier division enumerated everybody from the cradle to the grave, perhaps in anticipation of the government's social security programme. If a complete check were made of the 42,000 names on the lists we believe that at least 10,000 would prove to be false or improperly on the lists. From the information we have already it is
obvious that hundreds, perhaps several thousands. of names are improperly left off the lists.
In short, Mr. Speaker, I want to draw to the attention of the house my opinion that the lists are entirely useless at best, and at worst-and in Montreal, as I think hon. gentlemen will agree from the evidence that has been presented to this house from time to time -it is always the worst because Montreal has been a telegraphers' paradise-

speechtext:
I refer hon. members
to Hansard of June 29, 1934, page 4469, where an hon. gentleman whom I regard as being one of the ablest men who ever sat in this house made this statement:
I have had some experience in running elections in the city of Montreal, and as a matter of fact I do not employ voters in my own constituency; I employ voters who reside and vote in other constituencies, which is perfectly legitimate. As a matter of fact, if I am to conduct an election in the constituency of St. Lawrence-St. George, first I must have an inquiry to ascertain that the alleged voter resides where he says he resides. Then I must have some description of him so that he can be identified, and usually in order to identify him by questioning I wash to know his telephone number; if he has an office I wish to know where his office is situated and his office telephone number. I cannot run an election otherwise. In one of my elections a thousand voters were impersonated before they got to the polls. You must have means for a complete identification, and your representatives at the polls must be thoroughly informed so that they may prevent impersonation. At election time I employ people who do not vote in my constituency to do that clerical and protective work.
You must remember that if you are running an election in the city of Montreal you can go to an association in New York who will supply you with fifty or one hundred or two hundred or three hundred impersonators. These men will come to the city the day before the election, supplied with cards stating whom they are to impersonate; they will go from poll to poll impersonating voter after voter. In one election the only way we succeeded in preventing it was with the aid of a number of young men belong-
Dominion Elections

ing to athletic clubs, some of them associated with McGill university, who were active supporters of mine. They saw an automobile carrying five or six men; it would stop at one poll and one man would get out and vote; it would go to the next poll and another man would get out and vote; and we then discovered that they were imported personators. We took the law into our own hands and disabled each one of those automobiles, and defied the police to take charge of us for breaking the law in that way. So we were able to smash the combination. But there must be some way whereby money may be legitimately spent in investigating and informing ourselves with regard to prospective voters, in order to secure such information as will enable us to identify each and preserve his right to vote. I can only avoid the present law by going to some other constituency and engaging men there to do that preventive work for me. . . .
In one case I think we secured thirty or forty detectives from another province and some twenty or thirty others elsewhere. Strange to say, before the election I learned that even they were being bribed. We brought some sixty of them into the main committee room, told them we knew they were being bribed and were working for the opposite party and asked those who admitted it to take two paces to the front. Two-thirds of those men took two paces to the front, admitting that they were working for the other party and not for us. Such a situation is difficult but some way must be found to remedy it. I have evidence that at least fifty or sixty blank warrants were issued for use in my constituency. They were signed by a judge to be filled out when necessary. One committee in the St. Lawrence ward of my constituency of St. Lawrence-St. George, composed of respectable men, were arrested and put in gaol before the poll opened, through the use of blank warrants ostensibly signed by a judge in the city of Montreal. I have had police officers come to my main committee room where most representative women of the city were engaged on the telephones to persuade the voters to come to the polls. Those police officers had blank warrants which had been filled out on the street, -with which they attempted to come in and arrest the most representative people in the city. We have stood at the door and said we would use strong measures if they attempted to carry these warrants into effect, because we knew they were false and fraudulent. That sort of thing is carried on, and it is not surprising to find that in the constituency of St. Lawrence-St. George the election expenses have run up as high as $120,000 or $125,000 in a single election. I know of one case where the candidate contesting the election spent $75,000, and there was a contribution of $25,000 to the election fund which had never been reported to him.

speechtext:
Because that is the only place where I have any evidence before me to support such a charge. On Tuesday, July 6, there appeared in the Montreal Star a letter which was signed "Fair Play" complaining about the padding of the voters' lists. I have the clipping here, and I should like to put it; on record:
Sir,-I was greatly surprised the other night on reading the electoral list in my district to find, instead of two people in my house there are eleven listed. My neighbours next door have four people, and I saw fifteen names. Also there is a number added which does not even exist. Now, I ask you, does this mean all those people will vote under my address when there are really only two of us? We are not alone-

Dominion Elections
in this. Another person in this block is alone and yet five are shown by the list on the pole.
I think we ought to have some protection and also I think the people who canvass for names ought not to be allowed to do so unless they can spell properly as directed.
Then the reply by the returning officer for the electoral district of Cartier, Lazarus Bavitch, appeared in the Montreal Star of July 13, as follows:
Sir,-In connection with the recent complaint in your column by a voter in a certain poll in the electoral district of Cartier, with respect to the alleged padding of the list of voters in this poll, I desire, in my capacity as returning officer for the above electoral district, to draw to your attention the fact that I have personally investigated the poll in question in order to determine the accuracy of the complaint.
Upon investigation it was discovered that the pair of enumerators who had made up the list of this poll had unduly added to the list of names. The result of this investigation was forwarded by me to the chief electoral officer at Ottawa, who instructed me to appoint two new enumerators, in order to get an accurate list of names made of this poll. This enumeration is in the process of being completed. The fees of the original enumerators, which amounted to approximately $35 for each, have, accordingly, been forfeited.
These cases were brought to his attention, and he admits that the padding occurred; and apparently the only punishment that has been meted out to the persons who did this improperly, and against the law, is that they are to forfeit the $35 to which they were otherwise entitled. There are certain polls not referred to by the returning officer which are among the worst. A few moments ago I mentioned the situation that has arisen in certain of the divisions of Montreal. I quoted the words of Hon. C. H. Cahan and the admissions that were made before the parliamentary committee which sat during 1930 to 1935. Anyone who knows anything about the proceedings of that committee will recall that several outstanding cases of impersonation were mentioned. One other that is authenticated and often mentioned in Montreal is that on one occasion the Anglican bishop of Montreal, Bishop Farthing, appeared at his poll early on election day to vote, and was blithely informed that they were out of ballots, that all the ballots had been used up already, and, as it transpired, improperly; and that Bishop Farthing himself already had been voted for, that someone had voted in his name.

subtopic: BY-ELECTION IN CARTIER-ALLEGED IRREGULARITIES     MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I have made the statement, and I wish to repeat it, that allowing an election to be stolen and to be filched improperly is just as bad as setting aside elections altogether, that there is no difference between the robbing the people of the right to choose their own representatives freely, and the methods pursued by Adolf Hitler in Germany. The responsibility is on this House of Commons, and particularly on the government which is responsible for the conduct of affairs in this country, to take the appropriate action in these cases.
It may be said that revising officers are correcting the lists. As we know from experience, at this date that is a practical impossibility, when a situation as wholesale as this is revealed. Revising officers would quite properly require evidence before striking names off the list. It is patently impossible for all the electors themselves to check the lists and to appear before the revising officers for the necessary affidavit, and other evidence. Only a complete reenumeration of the constituency in question will meet the situation.
I would make the point quite strongly that unless the government does act it will have to take the responsibility for the irregularities in this forthcoming election. And now, knowing the facts, or at least some of the facts, it would be accessory to the crime both before and after the fact. It seems to me it is the duty of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King)-and I know the Prime Minister does

not countenance this sort of thing for a moment-to see to it that we cleanse this blot upon the record of democracy in Canada.
What can the government do? I am going to make some suggestions. I suggest that since the present returning officer-and this surely is quite improper-is a nephew of the Liberal candidate, and since he has already shown his complete incompetence in connection with this work, another returning officer or an assistant returning officer should be appointed, the latter to be selected by one of the other candidates. I suggest that the candidate first nominated or associated with a recognized party in this House of Commons might choose the assistant to the returning officer and, if you will, there should be a complete and immediate reenumeration of the constituency. This need not cause any delay. The new enumeration could be brought before the revising officer and, after taking the necessary legal steps as to evidence and so on, the revising officer could use the evidence so gathered to establish the official list for the election of August 9. The enumeration should be carried on in accordance with the law, by two enumerators at each poll, each representing an opposing party. If we look up the Dominion Elections Act, we find that section 17 of the Dominion Elections Act provides for this. This means that one enumerator per poll would represent the Liberal party, and one would represent the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, or the other national party in this by-election.

May I proceed, Mr. Speaker? The third point is that the government or the proper minister or officer should issue instructions requiring each voter to show his registration card at the poll. That might assist very materially.
I hope that the government will take steps which while they would be no guarantee of honesty would at least show that an attempt was being made to secure an honest election in the constituency of Cartier. Otherwise from what I have said this morning I think that the electors of that constituency will be overwhelmed by a corrupt and crooked election machine. I am not placing the responsibility upon any political party for that machine, but I am saying that it is the duty of this house
at this time to see that the forthcoming election in Cartier is as honest as we can make it and that those who have been responsible for this corruption and the placing of names improperly upon the voters' lists shall be prosecuted to the utmost extent of the law. To simply say to people who have padded the lists, "We are not going to pay you for the enumeration," is entirely insufficient. We have to safeguard democracy in this country and there is no way of bringing our democratic institutions into greater disrepute than to have the knowledge go abroad that this house, having information regarding the condition which exists in a constituency, does not take the proper action.

speechtext:
I heard the
statement made by Mr. Cahan in this house and he and I frequently talked together about the best methods of meeting some of these wholly improper and wrong practices which are adopted by certain people in elections,
Dominion Elections

but which certainly do not represent the wishes of members of this House of Commons. My hon. friend was good enough to say that he knew I would not approve of these methods. I think he might have said that with equal truth of every hon. member of this house. I believe that every member of parliament is interested in having honest elections, and I think every member of this House of Commons would be prepared to assist in seeing that elections are made as clean as it is possible to make them. My hon. friend says that if elections are to be stolen or filched, it is as bad as having no election at all. I would go further than that. I would say that it is worse than having no election at all because it is encouraging a form of wrongdoing that cannot be too quickly stamped out entirely, if representative institutions are to be respected in our country.
I did hear a day or two ago that some irregularity had occurred in connection with one of the enumerators or returning officers, but the particulars I do not recall at the moment. My colleague, the Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty), and I conferred about it at once, and the Secretary of State took steps immediately to have the chief electoral officer investigate the matter. This is the first intimation that I have had of anything of the kind to which my hon. friend has referred other than the one case I have just mentioned.
I wish to make it clear that the law under which elections are held, by-elections as well as general elections, is a law that was made by the parliament of Canada. I assume there is within the law itself the means of meeting a situation of this character. If there is not, then the House of Commons as a whole has been remiss in not seeing that the law was made sufficiently comprehensive to deal with anything of the kind. I shall be surprised if it is not, but I agree with my hon. friend when he says that there may be reasons why the government should insist where there are offences, where people are not complying to the full with the provisions of the law or taking steps which would defeat the purpose of legislation of this house, that everything possible is done to see that the situation is rectified and that wrongdoing is prevented as largely as possible.
I cannot say, speaking offhand at the moment, what is involved in the suggestions which my hon. friend has made as to the manner in which this situation can be most effectively dealt with, but I will say now that I shall take up the matter immediately with Other members of the government and that, as far as it is possible for the government so to do, steps will be taken to see that the 
election in Cartier is made as fair and square as it can possibly be made. I cannot express too strongly, not only on my own behalf but on behalf of my colleagues, and, may I say, on behalf of every member of this House of Commons, that not one of us in this House of Commons shall view as being warranted any situation with respect to by-elections that is not creditable to the country. I shall go further, and say that I do not care who the man is, whether he calls himself Liberal, Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, Social Credit or by any other designation, if he lends himself to practices that are wrong, he should be dealt with summarily without regard to anything except the offence of which he is guilty and circumstances relevant thereto. I shall be happy to assist in1 any way in my power toward seeing that, not only this election, but all elections, as far as possible, are conducted in a fair and honourable way.

speechtext:
I quite appreciate the
difference, Mr. Speaker, and I will limit my very few remarks to the point made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. He cited in support of his description of conditions in St. Lawrence-St. George the remarks of my predecessor, Hon. C. H. Cahan. These remarks were made in this house and before commiteees of this house, as I recall it, in 1934, and I have to remind hon. members that Mr. Cahan, for whom I had and have the utmost respect, used consistently to complain about the condition of affairs in St. Lawrence-
Dominion Elections

St. George, and equally consistently used to get elected there. He was elected in 1925, in 1926, and in 1930, and all that time he kept complaining steadily about conditions there. He said in his remarks quoted by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that he understood that some elections there had cost as much as $120,000 to $125,000, and the inference was always made that this money was spent in corrupting the electors. Well, I have to recall that in the last election Hon. Mr. Cahan was defeated by a not inconsiderable majority, and the expenses on both sides of the election on that occasion were lower than at any time in the history of the division, so far as expenses are known at all, and the expenses on the winning- side were considerably lower than those of the defeated side. Now, when the election began, when I was nominated, I went to Mr. Cahan and expressed my respect for him. I said, "This will be as clean a fight as we can make any election fight," and he agreed with that course. So far as I know, both of us lived up to that agreement completely. I never heard from anyone, Liberal or Conservative, inside or outside the constituency of any corruption or alleged corrupt practices during the election of 1940; and I think it is stretching a long bow to support an argument with regard to the Cartier division by making references to something said about St. Lawrence-St. George in 1934 by the member for that time.
I only conclude by saying that I think the people of St. Lawrence-St. George would support what I say, and that is that no election could have been cleaner than the last one, and I believe the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, who knows me pretty well, would agree that if I had anything to do with it that would be the case. I therefore submit Mr. Speaker, that the argument drawn over the boundary line from one division to another will not hold water for a minute.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BY-ELECTION IN CARTIER-ALLEGED IRREGULARITIES     MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I have no desire to take any lengthy part in the debate which has been initiated by the ihon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). However, I should like the house to know that my view is that the launching of this move to adjourn the house to discuss a matter of urgent public importance has served a useful purpose at an appropriate time.
As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) well pointed out, every member of this house, as every citizen in Canada, should be and is interested in seeing that we have honesty in our elections. That is a matter that goes to the very root of democracy, as the member for

Rosetown-Biggar pointed out. He went a good deal farther than that, indicating that this was the kind of thing which might perhaps be called a parallel to the disfranchisement of citizens generally and which, as he suggested, might lead to dictatorship. These are things which the average citizen and members of parliament must guard against with great jealousy, and the launching of this motion has brought to the house again the necessity for cleanliness and purity in our public life and in elections in Canada.
I was greatly surprised, indeed alarmed, to hear of the evidence which had been brought in affidavit form and otherwise by the hon. member for Rosetown-nBiggar. It indicates a situation which I can see, by his attitude, that the Prime Minister and others are anxious to clear up. This party takes the stand that matters of this kind must be cleaned up in the public interest, and we take that stand unequivocally.
I was interested in what the Prime Minister said in one of his asides, with reference to the historic constituency of North York, where he exhumed one of the old election corpses to bring it before the house, saying that there were some bus loads of people brought from Toronto, although he did not make it clear how they voted. Those who came by bus loads did not all vote for him. In any event I was pretty young at that time and was not able to take the keen interest that I do now in elections. It would be strange indeed, however, if all the wrongs were on one side, if all the sinners belonged to one political party, even in North York. I do not want to criticize the Prime Minister unduly for bringing up this matter, but the man against whom he ran in that election, and who perhaps was indirectly spoken of by the Prime Minister-I do not believe he meant it in that way-has passed away and he may be said to have left an excellent record in public and private service in Canada.
I wish to associate myself with those who have spoken in the interests of cleaner elections for Canada, and I suggest to the government that they should do all that lies in their power to go to the very root of the difficulties which have been brought before the house, to see that an example is made of this instance and to ensure that if such things occur in the future they will be dealt with to the full extent of the law.

speechtext: Listen to it and you will get somewhere.

subtopic: BY-ELECTION IN CARTIER-ALLEGED IRREGULARITIES     MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I would point out that the chief electoral officer has all the jurisdiction that is necessary to control this election, and if there have been such irregularities, as the hon. member who has moved the motion (Mr. Coldwell) has indicated, the writs should be cancelled or postponed and registration verified by the chief electoral officer and his deputies in the island of Montreal. With regard to the allegations made by the mover of the motion concerning the telegraphing of votes, people being left off the lists, and dead' voters, that is something that has gone on in almost every election that I have known of, because elections, as has been said, are not won with prayers. Registration cards should be produced by the voters. I suggest that anyone who cannot read or write should not be on the list.
In 1934 the then member for St. Lawrence-St. George headed a committee which revised the electoral law of the country, and many of the matters that have been referred to by the mover of the motion, which were prevalent throughout Canada, were thoroughly investigated. In 1930 in the constituency of St. Law-rence-St. George and west centre Toronto, some of these very things now complained of went on, and the particulars appeared in the daily press for a month after the elections. In Britain they have recognized, apart from two or three elections in Scotland, the principle of allowing a candidate representing the same party in a constituency to be elected for the duration of the war, but that practice will be prevented in Canada so long as anyone is a British subject and can deposit $200, an election will be held.
I submit that the chief electoral officer has absolute power, he is a thoroughly competent official and if there are irregularities as alleged,
the election could be postponed. The government has the power to suspend the election for thirty days or to cancel the writs until this situation is cleared up, if after investigation the complaints are justified.

speechtext:
I am not going to prolong the debate at any great length, but the matters that have been revealed this morning and which look rather damaging are the sort of thing that makes politics dirty. They are the sort of thing that makes democracy weak. Matters of this kind should be looked into with all sincerity and with a good purpose in view, and I do not think the purpose is served by merely blaming some enumerator who may not have carried on his work well or may eventually be proved to have padded some lists. I am inclined to think that where there are election corruptions the blame may be attached to some huge political party machine, and I suggest that in dealing with matters of this kind there should be such punishments as fit the crime. If we are to have honesty in our electoral system, then penalties must be imposed for breaking the law.
The Prime Minister has referred to this matter and has expressed his alarm and more or less indicated that it does not matter whether it is a Liberal candidate, a Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, a communist or any other candidate that is running. I am inclined to think that the responsibility should not always be attached to the candidate, but rather to the machinery that is behind, operating in these electoral campaigns. The matter brought up this morning casts the suspicion upon every member sitting in this house, not only from Montreal and district but from every other large metropolis in Canada, whether he is eligible to sit as the properly elected representative of the people.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has suggested'a way in which this matter can be dealt with, but I am not so sure that it goes far enough. I am wondering whether a thing of this kind should not be investigated more fully by the privileges and elections committee of this house.

It might suggest a doubt whether the government was sitting there by reason of corrupt electoral practices. I am not saying it is; of course not, but this matter is tremendously serious, so serious as to justify postponing the by-election until there has been a thorough investigation. And when that has been done, those found guilty of corrupt practices should not simply be allowed to run away, laughing up their sleeves. The strength of a law is to be found very often in the penalties it prescribes. Where there are no penalties and no punishment the law is often weak and ineffective.
The matter of registration cards has been brought into the discussion. I am not going into that in detail, but I do believe that a registration card should be shown- before a person is permitted to vote.

These little registration cards that we carry around in our pockets signed by somebody that nobody knows as deputy registrar, I am inclined to think are not worth very much. I believe a registration card should be issued under seal and be a document of value.

subtopic: BY-ELECTION IN CARTIER-ALLEGED IRREGULARITIES     MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I do not blame you, Mr. Speaker, for calling me to book. I know that was out of order. When the plebiscite was discussed we brought the same matter up and were told that we could not use registration cards on that occasion.
I will close by saying this. If our democratic system is to survive, our electoral system must be so framed that corrupt practices will be rendered well-nigh impossible, and until that is done we have not a democratic system at all. We are told that our boys are fighting to preserve democracy. Well, we had better get democracy here at home first before we talk in those terms, and if our democratic system is to be preserved, our electoral system must be safeguarded in every way so that corrupt electoral practices will become practically unknown.

Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): May I say a word to reassure the hon. member. The act provides penalties. Rule 11 of Schedule A to section 17 of Special Election Instructions says:
Enumerators who, wilfully and without reasonable excuse, omit from their list of electors the name of any person entitled to have his or her name entered thereon, or enter on the said) list the name of any person who is not entitled to have his or her name entered thereon, shall, in addition to any other punishment to which they may be liable, forfeit their right to payment for their services as enumerators.
Then section 70 (4) says:
When it is made to appear to the chief electoral officer that any election officer has been guilty of any offence against this act, it shall be his duty to make such inquiry as appears to be called for in the circumstances.
And he has further powers to intervene and incur such expenses as may be necessary for these purposes. Then subsection 5 provides:
The chief electoral officer shall have the like powers in the case of any offence which it is made to appear to him to have been committed by any person under section 17.
That is the section dealing with the enumeration. So that there are penalties provided by the act, and I can give the hon. member the assurance that all the facilities of the Department of Justice will be at the disposal of the chief electoral officer to see that prompt and appropriate penalties are meted out to anybody who may have violated the provisions of the act.

Mr. Speaker, I feel bound to rise to a question of privilege, as the result of a Canadian Press dispatch in the Winnipeg Free Press of July 17, in the following words:
Ask Board to Control Grains
Otawa, July 17 (CP)

The House of Commons agriculture committee, during a heated meeting in camera, approved yesterday a motion by E. E. Perley (Prog. Con., Qu'Appelle) that the Canadian wheat board be authorized to handle all oats and barley on a pooling basis according to grade, it -was learned last night.
The meeting approved a report to be submitted to the house, which will recommend additional encouragement to essential foods production.
Mr. Perley, supported by P. E. Wright (C.C.F., Melfort) and Robert Fair (N.D., Battle River), urged the committee to recommend a changed system of allocation of railway cars so that pool elevators in Saskatchewan would receive better treatment. The members claimed' there was discrimination against these cooperative elevators.
I tabled the reports of the committee on agriculture and colonization this morning, and I wish to say, first, that I did not give out any report of the meeting referred to in the press, or disclose the contents of the committee's report to any member of the press. In fact, no member of the press ever approached me with respect to it. Second, the report which I tabled to-day, which is the committee's report, does not recommend that the Canadian wheat board be authorized to handle all oats and barley. Third, the meeting, while held in camera as are all committee meetings when considering draft reports, was not a heated meeting, as the dispatch implies. Fourth, according to a letter from the chairman of the wheat board, and read to the committee, no complaint had been received that the distribution of cars was unsatisfactory until June 18, following his appearance before the committee; and that since then several conferences had been held in an attempt to bring about a more satisfactory and workable system. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce by reason of the approach of the new crop season. My question has to do with what is being done with respect to the proper allocation of freight cars, particularly in areas in the prairie provinces where all or part of the threshing was not completed last fall, with the result that many of the farmers in those areas are unable to dispose of their wheat. I believe I should give the minister an example setting out the situation in one particular area, namely, Davidson, Saskatchewan. During the past twelve days only ten cars have been loaded at Davidson. There are 125,000 bushels of wheat to be marketed on the fifteen-bushel quota. Those who did not get threshed until this spring have been able to market very little, and it is going to be a great hardship on them if they cannot get their quota on the market before the new crop comes in. I am informed that in other areas where marketing has taken place, cars are still being received. My question is this: What is being done in this regard to assure an equitable and fair allocation of cars, and in particular is preference being given to areas in which farmers were unable to sell wheat last fall, because of the lateness of the threshing season, or in which threshing was not completed until this spring?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: ALLOTMENT OF FREIGHT CARS TO WESTERN CANADA -LABOUR-AVAILABILITY OF ELEVATOR SPACE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's question has to do with a situation which is causing us very considerable concern at the present time. I refer to the matter of the aceptance of farmers' quotas in western Canada. A great deal of the difficulty at first was that of transportation. That has been a serious situation, and has developed to the point where at the present time there are some 4.500 railway cars loaded with wheat at Fort William waiting for emptying. Including that 4,500 there are a total of some 13,000 cars at Fort William and elsewhere loaded with some 18,000,000 bushels of wheat. This situation, as I say, was at first a transportation difficulty. Recently however it has developed largely into a matter of labour. The ability to get labour at the head of the lakes is the difficulty. My department, the Department of Labour and other branches of goverment concerned have, obviously, been giving this matter anxious and serious attention. I am informed that the labour situation looks as if it will reach an early solution.
Wheat

Of the 1,000 Canadian civilians known to be in Japan and Japanese occupied China, 163 are known to be interned. Mr. Chairman, at the outset I wish to say that this question, of farm debts bids fair to remain, as it has been since 1935, a political football. I am not unmindful of the fact that one provincial government in this dominion obtained power by promises of what it would do if put into
Farmers' Creditors Act

power in that province: I refer of course to Alberta. If the farm debt question was not regarded as a vote getter, much of the talk which we have heard on this bill would never have taken place, and I feel confident that the vast majority of farmers in western Canada will appraise at their true worth the adulatory remarks which have been made with respect to them by certain hon. gentlemen connected with the Social Credit and Cooperative Commonwealth Federation parties. I was astounded at the lengths to which some hon. members have gone in fulsome praise of all farmers in western Canada. One hon. member was so good as to say that all of them were honest, efficient and industrious. I recommend to those hon. gentlemen that when they go back to their constituencies they talk with some of the farmers there about their neighbours. They know very well, and the records prove, that such a statement is wholly false in fact. I for one do not believe, speaking by and large, that farmers as such are any more honest than lawyers-that is, members of my own profession-and I do not believe that all lawyers are honest. The same is true equally with regard to preachers-

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I question that statement.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: You would not be willing to debate it, though?

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
and teachers, and business men, and insurance men; not all of them are honest. Fortunately we have laws of general application which take care of the dishonest, the lazy and the unthrifty, and where such laws are not applicable, nature often steps in and takes care of the situation. I suggest that hon. members approach this problem with a practical sense of its implications, and of the damage which may be done to those who do not now and never will claim the alleged benefits of this legislation.
Circumstances do arise in which by reason of unpredictable conditions, special legislation is necessary. This condition arose so far as agriculture is concerned in western Canada in the late 'thirties, when the then leader of the Conservative party, a man whom I delight to honour as my predecessor, the hon. member for West Calgary, and a former prime minister of this dominion, introduced and passed with the approval of this house a farmers' creditors arrangement act to take care of those special circumstances and conditions-conditions whose effects were spread not only over the west but all through agricultural Canada. The act as then passed was made of general application. It was designed to help whom?

Everybody? All farmers? No; only those who could satisfy a tribunal, set up for the purpose of adjudicating thereon, that they were unable, through circumstances beyond their control as efficient, industrious and honest farmers, to meet their debts as they came due. That act has been in operation for nine years in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, and despite that fact, despite the fact that the door was wide open to any and every farmer who felt that he could comply with the simple conditions set forth in the-act, despite the availability of these boards and the simplicity of the procedure, less than ten percent of the farmers have availed themselves of the privilege or opportunity presented by this legislation.
Now, why be so much concerned about the ten or at the very outside fifteen per cent of your farming population being unable to meet their debts as they become due? Have we similar special legislation with regard to other sections or classes of the community? The answer is definitely in the negative. I suggest that the fact that the other provinces of' Canada took early steps to have the act removed from application to their provinces should make us pause and consider. The fact that, as I now understand!, there are so few applications before the boards at the present time should give us reason to pause and consider whether or not this legislation should be passed at all. I may say quite frankly that but for the limitations in the bill as to the debts to which it will apply, I for one would not support the passing of the bill. I believe that in our attempt to help ten per cent, or fifteen per cent at the very outside, of our farming community in western Canada, we may do irreparable harm to the other eighty-five or ninety per cent of the farmers of the west, and it is on their behalf that I am prompted to speak as I do this afternoon. All the implications of this bill will be felt in our post-war period so far as the vast majority of our farming population is concerned.
As the member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews) so well said last night, and as the premier of Manitoba eloquently and logically stated in the address which the hon. member quoted, credit is based upon confidence. That is the keystone of the arch, not only of commercial and industrial but of agricultural relations and in all our business relations generally. It is not difficult for you and me to find out what our credit is. If you have any doubts about that, ask your friend, ask your neighbour how much he will lend you.

Farmers' Creditors Act
I do suggest that credit and confidence are based on knowledge, character and past dealings, and if we are dishonourable, if our record is bad, then our credit as such is gone. If it is to be bruited abroad that a first mortgage or an agreement fo" sale has no validity in a court of British justice, by reason of an act of this parliament interfering with contractual obligations, then I for one would not want to invest my money or my savings or earnings in any venture founded on real estate security in the province of Alberta.
The implications of this bill go farther than one individual case. I dare say we are all aware that in years gone by people have invested their money or saved it by buying life insurance, and they look to those policies to provide for them, for those whom they love and who are dependent upon them in their later years, or when they are gone and1 yet I know, as does everyone here, that the insurance policy which is to be a protection for me in my old age, and for my dependents, cannot be paid, it cannot be matured unless the mortgages in western Canada are paid with interest. I wonder how many of us would be in favour of this legislation if there were introduced concurrent legislation to provide that the life insurance companies, which are the great repository of trust funds in Canada, were to be relieved of their contractual obligations, to pay your wife or your dependent children, or yourself in your old age, the amounts stipulated for in the contract.
I say therefore that this legislation has a much wider implication than the province of Alberta, or Saskatchewan or Manitoba. I for one would like to believe that the insurance companies with whom I have been depositing my premiums from year to year were spending some portion of that money in helping responsible farmers, business men and industrialists in the province of Alberta; and yet I would be the first to rise and condemn them if under existing legislation, or legislation as we have had it in that province for the last ten years, any insurance company had invested my life savings in a first mortgage in Alberta, or in an agreement for sale, or even in provincial government bonds. I am sure that upon a realization of that fact the same criticism would fall from your lips. This is extraordinary, exceptional legislation. It interferes with contractual rights and obligations, regard and respect for which go to the very roots of our economic system in the English-speaking world. This is essentially class legislation, and as such should be viewed not only from the standpoint of the comparatively few citizens of the
class who will benefit, but from the effect which it will have on the rest of the class, on the rest of the farmers who constitute the vast majority of the people of western Canada, and upon our citizenry as a whole.
Confidence is the basis of all credit. Without credit western Canada would not have developed as it has in the last thirty years, and without credit western Canada cannot hope to keep pace with the rest of the dominion in the post-war years.
Coming to the farmers of western Canada themselves, while I do not and have not acted for many years for any so-called investment companies, mortgage or life insurance companies, I did have in the earlier years of my practice, in the years succeeding 1920, from 1921 to 1925, considerable to do with mortgage foreclosures. I did act for one mortgage company and that experience served to confirm me in my belief in one thing, and that is the absolute impartiality and fairness and essential justice of our courts in dealing with mortgage foreclosures. I foreclosed from one hundred to one hundred and fifty mortgages in that time. That is a conservative estimate. In no instance was the foreclosure opposed. In no instance was there by any stretch of the imagination one dollar of equity in the land for the borrower. In every instance the mortgage company took losses varying from a few hundred to several thousands of dollars.

speechtext:
The farmers' equity had gone, if you will, "with the wind". In many instances the farmer had abandoned his land. It was my usual practice to make inquiries of the secretary of the municipality, the school board or the reeve of the municipality in regard to the character and ability and industry and thrift and honesty of the farmer whose mortgage was being foreclosed. In no instance that I can recall was there any protest by any neighbour or by any responsible man in the community as to the impropriety of the proceedings which had to be taken. It is not surprising to know that that mortgage company is no longer in business. It failed-and there is no legislation to take care of it.
My second observation is this. I have amongst my clientele numbers of elderly people, retired farmers, if you will, men who sold their farms because of age or infirmity. One of the most distressing things to me is to find an old couple who have spent their years in developing and paying for a farm in Saskatchewan, in one instance, in Alberta
Farmers' Creditors Act

in another, now living on relief and charity by reason of the application of this act, which wiped out their equity in their farm and left them without a roof over their heads that they could call their own. They are now dependent on the bounty of the province. In the one instance that comes most vividly to my mind a farmer came in from across the line, not a Canadian citizen, and bought this farm for $2,000 cash and a promise to pay the balance, not in cash but in so many thousands of bushels of wheat in succeeding years. And now he carries on secure in his tenure on a farm on which he has lived for only four or five years. He has changed his method of farming and gone into live stock, cattle and hogs, and lives in comparative luxury on the farm which the farmer and his wife homesteaded while they exist in homeless penury. .
It works both ways. There are not a few farmers in Saskatchewan and Alberta who would gladly sell their farms but for this act and similar legislation that has been in existence in the province. Now, perforce, they will not sell unless they get all cash. Young men are growing up in our province to-day who would willingly and gladly buy a farm and establish a home, but they cannot do it because they cannot get the credit. Their neighbours, men who have known them all their lives, older men, say: I cannot sell to you for fear of this very legislation. The result is that we are doing the very thing that some hon. gentlemen who spoke last night deplored. We are creating a condition in those western provinces which can lead to nothing but a population of tenant farmers. I could name a dozen men to-day in good districts in Alberta who would gladly sell their farms but for this and similar legislation. But now it is "all cash or nothing". And why? Because the farmer who owns his land says: This farm is all I have to take care of me, and you may make an agreement to pay me one-third of the crop up to five or ten thousand, or whatever the case may be. But to-morrow or next year you may walk into the debt adjustment office and take advantage of this legislation, and I shall no longer have my home or security; the payments on which I was relying to keep me in my old age will not be forthcoming, so that I prefer not to sell, and I shall rent my farm instead, as so many other farmers have done and are doing. The same thing is true in connection with the lands which have been foreclosed in years gone by; no mortgage or investment company will lend money on farm mortgages 
or discount agreements for sale, for the very reason I have mentioned. What, is the foundation of all credit? It is confidence.
I commend the minister for the legislation he has introduced. I commend him on the limiting clauses which are contained in that legislation for, as I see the prospects ahead, with the prosperity we have in western Canada at the present time, with the record now before us as to the reduction and liquidation of farm debts and obligations, in another three, four or five years this legislation will go into the discard, because no longer will it bj necessary. Then I trust that the confidence of the investing public in western Canada will be restored and that we shall go ahead side by side with our sister provinces, participating to the fullest extent in the prosperity which I believe lies ahead of this the finest country in the world.

I think I can say I take just a little pleasure in following the hon. member for Calgary West. The hon. gentleman has made one or two very singular statements. To me he seemed particularly interested in the welfare of insurance companies and other financial institutions, and I wondered if he had forgotten that the legislation we are now discussing is supposed to be designed to settle debt, not to protect any investment funds he may have in the form of premiums deposited with insurance companies. The unfortunate thing about his exposition this afternoon is that evidently he is in a happier position than many others, in that he has some little investment in the form of life insurance premiums. As I understand it, this debt legislation is designed to protect the unfortunate farmer who never in the wide world will be able to build up any security for his o'ld age in terms of insurance.
The hon. gentleman said that he has never represented any financial institution. Well, I should say that he could not have done a better job of representing them than he did in his speech this afternoon. I believe the hon. gentleman should have thought a little more deeply than evidently he has been thinking in the past. He had a good deal to say about the credit of Alberta; in the first place he had a good .deal to say about confidence. The very word "confidence" is a misnomer unless we are told in what we are to have confidence. The hon. gentleman uyas speaking as though the investment corporations had no confidence in the Alberta government. Well, I am not going to say whether they have or have not; if the hon. gentleman wishes to speak in those terms, that is all right with me. While he was speaking, however, I rather fancied that he imagined himself on the opposition side

Farmers' Creditors Act
in the Alberta legislature. The hon. member for Acadia reminds me to ask the hon. gentleman whether he has ever read the report of the Bank of Canada following the investigation it made into the Alberta situation a few years ago. I have not the exact words before me, but that report placed almost the entire blame for the loss of credit upon former administrations in that province, particularly those administrations under the Liberal regime. However, I shall not now bring up that old stuff. I should like to know, however, in what the hon. gentleman means we should have confidence. Surely there is not a mortgage company which would not have confidence in an agricultural policy which gave farmers adequate prices for their produce. I suggest that the hon. member's thinking is a little shallow there, and I believe he should go a little further under the surface.
Let us look at the matter in this way. If in Canada there could be an agricultural policy which would keep agriculture solvent, therein would lie all the confidence of which any investors would ever have need. I suggest that if in the past the Alberta government took certain action to protect the farmers, it was not because it had any grievance against the mortgage companies or lending institutions, but because this Ottawa government, which is responsible for national policy, never had a national agricultural policy that kept agriculture solvent at all times. I think the hon. member should look at matters in that light, instead of playing politics to the gallery. Let me remind the hon. member of this: If agriculture in Alberta had been solvent there would have been no need for the government of that province in days gone by to tackle so vigorously the debt situation as it existed there. The only reason they tackled it was that the farmers were being driven off their land and out of their homes. Surely the sanctity of a farm home is as sacred as some sort of financial scheme. That is the way we must look at the operation of the present fiscal policy of the country.
We have no quarrel with the lending institutions. They are all well and good in their proper place. Our quarrel is with a bad financial policy, with finance itself, with monetary arrangements which have existed and continue to exist. I believe I can say that, after all, the basic trouble of practically all our problems, even to the extent of1 our international problems, is one of finance.
Since the hon. member for West Calgary has mentioned Alberta, may I point out that ever since it took office in 1935 the Alberta government has laboured hard and battled well to alleviate the most distressing agricultural debt situation one could imagine. As
early as 1937 the government of that province passed what was known as the Credit of Alberta Regulation Act. This was basic legislation which, we believe, would have enabled the government of Alberta to deal with the debt problem. But what happened to this legislation? It was immediately disallowed by the central government here at Ottawa. Following that the Alberta government passed a measure known as the Reduction and Settlement of Debt Act. This act would have established a basis of settlement for all outstanding debts. But what happened to that legislation? It was declared by the courts to be ultra vires of the province. Then came what is known as the Home-Owners Security Act. This was passed because, under the stress of world conditions and, shall I say, a falsified financial system over which individuals had no control whatsoever, many were forced to mortgage their homes, and were then in danger of losing them. Surely it should be recognized that there can be no sanctity of contract which does not also recognize the sanctity of human life and homes. Surely the sanctity of homes has as least as much value as the consideration of a faulty money system. This act, too, was disallowed by the central government at Ottawa. If it had been allowed to stand it would have brought debtor and creditor together to seek an equitable basis of settlement through the medium of a debt adjustment board. The farmers of Alberta would not have been faced with the present situation had that act not been disallowed.
That is our contention, and has been from that day to this. The argument has gone on as to whether or not the debt adjustment board had the right to settle debts. This issue was thrown out, not only by the courts of Canada but by the privy council. This, Mr. Chairman, is the record of a great battle against a great power. And I will say this, that the late William Aberhart started the battle for the emancipation of the people from slavery and debt. That battle is not yet won, but, may I say to the committee through you, Mr. Chairman, the battle is not yet lost, either. We are going to continue to fight on against a faulty money system, a financial power which, after all, is the greatest power and enemy of the people in the world.
I believe I should say that the responsibility in connection with farm debt does not lie altogether upon the shoulders of the farmers. It seems to me that the lending institutions must bear their fair share of the responsibility. The farmer is no more responsible for the weather, for the drought, for the grasshoppers,

Farmers' Creditors Act

for the hail or for the frost than is the lending institution. But of course the lending institution must be protected in some way or another, while the farmer is left to do the best he can, under conditions of uncertainty.
I bold in my hand a brief entitled "Abuses of Arbitrary Debt Adjustment," put out by the Dominion Mortgage and Investments Association. I believe it was referred to a few days ago. In this brief we find set out a number of examples, and I should like to read only a few words for purposes of illustration. This is what I find at page 7:
A loan of $800 was made on a quarter-section (160 acres) in 1928. In the 12 years prior to the Board of Review hearing, the borrower paid $131 to the mortgagee and $31 on account of taxes, an average of $13.50 a year. At the end of 12 years, in addition to the $800 which had been loaned him. he owed $119 for insurance premiums, etc., $623 interest and $366 tax arrears. If he had had no mortgage he would have still gone behind more than $200 on his taxes alone.
Before going further I would point out that the lending institution lent the money to this farmer. Surely they would know something about him, the location of his farm and whether or not it was productive. But notice what happens. The brief goes on to state: Neither the amount of the loan, the interest rate nor anything else in connection with his mortgage has any material bearing on this man's difficulties.
Well, that is all right; we agree with that statement. I believe it would be true in almost every case. Perhaps farmers have been treated fairly well; perhaps mortgage companies have attempted to settle debts equitably, so long as they were protected and did not lose any money. I am not saying they did not. So that phase of the brief is quite all right. But notice this part:
The facts speak for themselves. Evidence tendered showed that the debtor was an inefficient farmer unable to manage bis farm or personal affairs.
Yet the lending institution lent money to this farmer. Surely they should have known something about the farmer at the time. Then it goes on to say:
His land is admittedly poor and low grade. Did the mortgage company not know that before they lent the money?
As a productive self-contained unit it is never likely to produce sufficient to maintain this family, let alone pay off any debt or taxes.
Yet the lending company lent the money.
It has, however, a value of at least $1,100 as an adjunct to an adjoining farm.
It would appear from that simple statement that just so long as the lending company is secured, it is not very much concerned about 
the welfare of the farmer or the question whether or not he can pay his debts. If it had been, it would have safeguarded its interests before it ever lent the money. When companies do that sort of thing surely they have some responsibility if it works out that the farmer, doing the best he can with poor land and gambling against the price of wheat, frost, drought, grass-hoppers and all the other things that enter into the uncertainty of farming, cannot meet his burden of debt.
The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) has handed to me a Bank of Canada report on the financial position of the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, 1937. This is what that report says in respect of Alberta on page 34:
After making full allowance for the rapid economic development of the new province, and the legitimate cost of facilities provided by the government to aid and stimulate this development, it remains the case-in our opinion- that the 1905-22 period was characterized by waste, loose administration, and incurrence of debt to an extent which could not be justified even when allowance is made for the optimistic spirit of the times.
That period of the provinces' history was governed by a Liberal administration. I thank the hon. member for Acadia for handing me that report. The hon. member for Calgary West can think over that should he ever be suffering from insomnia any of these nights.
I should like to say something that perhaps has been said already. I am at a loss to know why the Minister of Finance has evidently ignored the recommendations of the debt- conference which was called by the three western provinces. The premiers of these provinces met together and forgot politics. Mr. Bracken who was then premier of Manitoba, Premier Aberhart of Alberta and Premier Patterson of Saskatchewan, forgot their political differences and joined hand to hand in a debt conference. They arrived at certain conclusions and they presented a draft bill. Those premiers subsequently came down and interviewed the government, but so far as this present legislation is concerned it would appear that their representations have been entirely ignored. Since we are in committee I would ask the minister to tell us why he ignored the recommendations of that conference of premiers. In addition to that, farm organizations have submitted briefs of one kind and another, but evidently they have been ignored in this legislation.
This whole situation will never be cleared up by simply passing debt legislation of this kind; the whole debt problem will have to be tackled in a different way. Last fall

Farmers' Creditors Act
a conference was held in Winnipeg on postwar reconstruction, and one paragraph of the resolution dealing with private and industrial debts reads as follows:
Therefore, be it resolved that all agricultural mortgage debts be taken over by an agricultural credit bank operating under a national monetary authority, on the following basis:
(a)	The principal amount of debts to be reduced to the original indebtedness less all payments made in excess of three per cent. The farmer will be required to pay this to the agricultural credit bank in equitable instalments on a crop or production share basis.
(b)	The agricultural credit bank will repay creditors on equitable terms which will ensure that individuals incur no loss and corporations can meet their liabilities in full.
If something like that were done, the hon. member for Calgary West would need to have no misgivings that any insurance company, mortgage company or any other lending institution would go broke.
