subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Representing a province which is both industrial and agricultural, I wish to say a few words on the inequality of this proposed national policy for debt reconstruction in Canada, growing out of the principle laid down in the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act which was passed by parliament in 1934 during the period of depression and drouth. The government of that day adopted a courageous course in an endeavour to help the farmers on the prairies, and in 1938 all the provinces were excluded with the exception of Alberta and Saskatchewan.
I have been a critic of the loan companies, insurance companies and mortgage companies in this country, and when I saw the amendments that were introduced in 1938 in connection with the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and saw at the same time that war was almost inevitable, I predicted that the provincial debt legislation would be upset on appeal to the privy council. That prediction was fulfilled, as everyone knows.
What I object to with regard to this whole question is this. It would be far better for the government to adopt a truly national policy of debt readjustment to protect the equities not only of the farmers of western Canada but of other classes of the population. A policy of debt reduction and the conservation of equities, as well as the readjustment of differences between mortgagors and mortgagees, would be a truly national policy if it brought within its scope all classes from coast to coast including farmers, fishermen, industrial workers and the white collar workers in the cities and towns, and market gardeners. Ontario seems to be the forgotten province of confederation. It is a large agricultural province, as well as a large industrial centre, but it has been entirely overlooked by the government in the matter of debt readjustment.
The Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act has been administered in a haphazard manner by the various boards throughout the country, so that there has not been equality in the attempt to relieve the burdens of those who have been suffering from debts. When the war began I had a motion on the order paper in which I proposed a national moratorium in Canada, and I suggest that it would have been far better as a means of protecting the equities of the Canadian people, because the system which we are now considering protects the equities of some and ignores the equities of other classes. I proposed a truly national policy of debt reduction instead of the system we have here, which is one of state socialism for a section of the community and not for others. This is a federal measure, and if we are going to conserve the interests of some
people in Canada we should do the same for the whole population, in a real national policy, including those engaged in industrial pursuits. It should apply particularly to the primary producers-lumbermen, fishermen, farmers and those engaged in the industrial life of Canada. The bill before us, however, does not aim at anything so equitable.
It is proposed that certain judges shall take charge of the administration of this bill when it becomes law. This, I suggest, will prove as fatal as the mistakes that were made under the original Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. The purpose is to rescind the 1934 act, which now applies only to Alberta and Saskatchewan; the explanation given in the explanatory note is that it is intended to consolidate and re-write the act so as to make it applicable to certain classes of farmers, namely, those on the prairies, and to include Manitoba in the new debt adjustment scheme.
In the past I have also made certain proposals, which I thought would prove of benefit to the Canadian people, with regard to the shark loan companies. I suggested that there should be a national moratorium on all equities and that the rate of interest should be fixed at 5 per cent or less, or in any event that there should be a lower rate than those which were being charged. Just consider the lot of our industrial workers in the cities and towns. What is going to become of these people at the close of the war? They are going to lose their jobs altogether, their equity will be gone, and during the period of conversion from war-time to peace-time standards over a number of years there will be a large number of Canadian workers without employment. We know what happened after the last war. At that time nearly 600,000 people from the farms and from various occupations in the cities and towns of Canada found it necessary to migrate to the United States to look for work. I am afraid the same thing will happen after this war, but the situation will be more serious. The government, therefore, should try in a national scheme to preserve the equities of all our people and not just those of a particular section.
I quite appreciate the condition of the farmers on the prairie. They have had to face long years of drought and depression, and two wars, and they have seen the prices of their products fall to an alarming degree; wheat had gone down from $1.50 to 34 cents or thereabouts, and they have had to pay high prices for the things they have had to buy. I deeply sympathize with them, and so did the Conservative government in 1934 when they brought down the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act to meet the condition that
Farmers' Creditors Act

prevailed at that time of depression and drought.;' That act had been weighed in the balance and found wanting, but I do not think that the new proposed measure will help matters vefiy much.
I have received a number of pamphlets from mortgage and loan companies, and I admit that there is a degree of justice in some of the statements they make. I quote:
The debt legislation suggested by the governments of the three prairie provinces is so drastic in character that it would completely destroy western farm credit and would mean that for alt, practical purposes there would be no such tHihg as a farm mortgage.
There is need for curtailment rather than an extension of farm debt legislation. The Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act was passed in 1934 as a temporary measure to meet a temporary emergency, but the emergency has passed and the position of western farmers has improved very materially. Cash income of Manitoba and Alberta farmers is greater than in the prosperous 1926-1929 period.
The farm debt situation is greatly exaggerated in some quarters in western Canada. Half of the farms have no mortgage debt and only a small percentage are burdened with debt. Deserving borrowers already have ample protection from harsh creditors and there is no danger of a flood of foreclosures.
The real owners of farm mortgages held by a savings institution such as a life insurance company are the policyholders. There are far more policyholders than there are borrowers on a mortgage and this is true not only for the country as a whole but for western Canada itself. Unnecessary losses brought about by debt legislation come out of the pockets of policyholders.
Let us not forget that some of the mortgages are held by private persons, widows and others. I have no objection to the principle of the bill, but, I repeat, there are other people in Canada who need similar assistance. Our industrial workers will suffer when this war is over, if not before. But the owners of real estate are also faced with a problem and there is no similar protection for them. Nearly everyone in this house has real estate of some description. In our cities and towns to-day no one wants to own real estate because there is no protection for the owner. The minister comes along and appoints a rent controller and makes it impossible by the regulations . he passes for any man to administer his property as he should from the commercial aspect. He cannot get any real revenue from it because he is hemmed in by controllers and subcontrollers. Why is his equity also not included in this bill? Some of the mortgagees in the cities and towns are charging 61 per cent and we know that for years the shark loan companies have been charging two per cent per month and sometimes three per cent. They have also asked for chattel mortgages and bills , of sale as

collateral, and have been in effect a lot of tax collectors. What chance has the industrial worker, the urban or suburban worker, and the market and truck gardener?
This pamphlet, "The Prairie Farmer and His Debts", says at page 9, that the borrowers need a sound mortgage law. If I had my way I would have a sound mortgage law under which the rate of interest would be four and a half or five per cent, with a national moratorium for everyone for the war period, if necessary, because everybody wants to pay his debts. But some of these mortgage companies are charging six and a half per cent, and that should be impossible to-day. Speaking of the legislation which has been proposed to the dominion government for the adjustment of farm debts in the prairie provinces and its defects and dangers, this pamphlet says:
If enactedi, it would destroy western farm credit. It would also have very far reaching effects on existing farm mortgages in western Canada. For all practical purposes it would mean that there is no such thing as a farm mortgage. Present and future mortgages and agreements for sale would be nothing more than a promise to pay-
They mean it will become a scrap of paper, no doubt.
-the amount and conditions of payment to be determined by a non-judicial tribunal from whose arbitrary -decision there will presumably be no appeal as is the case under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act.
The effect of the legislation would be to make all contracts with western farmers one-sided. A mortgage or other written contract would have little meaning. There would be little point in making a loan to a farmer by way of a mortgage or in selling a farm under an agreement for sale. The creditor or vendor would be bound, but the debtor or purchaser would not. No matter what contract was executed by the debtor, the creditor would have no security though he will have parted with his money or property. Such legislation would make mortgages a nullity and' would in fact abolish mortgages by removing every vestige of the legal rights which have always characterized them.
Western farmers themselves would suffer from such legislation. Farmers desiring to retire would hesitate to sell their farms, except for all cash or with very substantial cash down payments. The risk of doing so would be too great for the amount and terms of payment would be uncertain. Would-be purchasers, except those with substantial capital, would be unable to buy farms. This, in fact, is very much the situation which prevails to-day though existing debt legislation does not apply to new contracts. The reason for this is the fear that the legislation may be changed to apply to new as well as old contracts. It is now apparent that this fear is justified, the proof being the legislation which has -been proposed to the dominion government. This proposed legislation would place restrictions on the rights of creditors under all contracts whether existing or future.

Farmers' Creditors Act
I say in all fairness to the workers of this country that there should be equality of treatment between the urban and suburban workers and the workers on the farm, instead of letting one man's equity be wiped out while the other man's equity has the protection of a statute. That is not a fair proposition. There should be equality of treatment. That was one of the weaknesses of the act of 1934, and I raised this very question when our own government was in power. I said that it was most unfair and unequitable to the industrial workers in our cities and towns that they should not be given the same equality of treatment as was afforded to the farming population-and in 1935 fishermen were added-under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. But the industrial workers are given no such relief.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
This legislation does not apply particularly to Ontario, because we freed ourselves from it back in 1938, and I am sure it is a good thing for agriculture that we did; for I consider this bad legislation. After all, Canada is a young country and we would do well to look very carefully at this type of legislation which more or less legalizes dishonesty. We are trying in this young nation to develop a character for honesty and traditions of good citizenship to hand down to posterity, and I sometimes wonder what they will think of legislation of this type which does not honour contracts. I make my appeal not only from the point of view not only of the good of the nation but also of the good of the honest-to-goodness farmer who many find himself deprived of credit because of the record established by those who have taken advantage of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. No doubt some good has been accomplished by the act, but we have paid very dearly for it. When someone has been kind enough to lend his substance, an honest effort should be made to repay the loan, and I do not see why a loan should not be repaid to a mortgage company just as much as to an individual. Unfortunately one can hardly speak of financial institutions if one comes from Ontario without being branded as a defender of the big interests. Let me say that I have no interest whatsoever in any loan company. I am thinking only of the welfare of the honest-to-goodness farmer who may need some credit in the post-war period, and from his point of view I say that this legislation in the main has been bad legislation.
The Minister of Finance is to be congratulated upon having removed from the act some Of the vices which brought discredit on agriculture. I yield to no man in my diesire to
serve the agricultural industry. But we' must take a long term view of it. We as farmers cannot be continually branded as people who refuse to assume our obligations if we expect to retain our dignity and self-respect. I say that this legislation was a great handicap to the prosperity of agriculture in Ontario.
I listened with interest to the hon. member for Macleod. He felt there should be some way of tackling this debt problem. I say frankly that the only way of tackling the debt problem is by sacrifice, thrift and honesty, and restoring the loans to- those who have been kind enough to lend of their substance. There may be those who through unfortunate circumstances get into a position where they cannot pay, but it must be remembered that the loans which have been made to agriculture created assets in those farms if the money was wisely spent, and those farms should in consequence have increased in value.
I listened with interest to the hon. member for North Battleford. She mentioned the case of a man who had homesteaded on a farm and had raised fourteen children and afterwards became insolvent and could not retain his home. But, after all, that person had the use of that land, and is there any hon. member who would not exchange one hundred acres of land for fourteen children? I think he did get some value after all, because while he was on that farm he raised fourteen children. We must look at both sides of the question if we are to be fair.
I read the remarks which the hon. member for Yorkton made on this bill. He said that debt is the natural result of the capitalist system, and that under this system the reward of capital always comes first, and the reward to labour has to take care of itself. Well, Mr. Speaker, what is capital? As I see it, the,difficulty in many of these controversial questions is that it depends on whose ox is being gored. After all, capital is nothing but stored up labour; and if the nation is to be served by capital it is necessary to put that labour to work, whether it is in the form of money or in any other form. After all, it is necessary for this country to be developed, and it is necessary that this stored up labour be used. The unfortunate thing is that as long as this world is peopled by human beings there will be envy and jealousy. The man who made sacrifices, who in his early days went without things; the man whose father or grandfather pioneered with the idea of making the world1 a better place in which his descendants might live, now is looked upon with envious eyes by those who think he is travelling rather an easy road,
Farmers' Creditors Act

when the very people who criticize him very often are the ones who would refuse to make sacrifices themselves in order to store up some of this labour, to put themselves in the position of a creditor instead of that of a debtor. This may be hard language to use to hon. gentlemen across the way, andt I should be rather reluctant to make these statements but for the fact that on almost every measure that comes up in this house we have to listen to pious, hypocritical expressions in regard to honesty and dishonesty; and then it turns out that they want some back-door method by means of which dishonesty may serve their purposes, when they have not enough stamina to make the sacrifices that have been made by others. These things may serve their own purposes, but they do great harm to the industry of agriculture.
I am satisfied that the farmer himself can usually handle his own problems. I do not understand why in the western provinces so many of these loans have come into the hands of the large corporations. Surely there are individuals who have saved money. Why do they not lend to their neighbours as we have done in Ontario? By virtue of their sacrifices the pioneers in this country accumulated funds which they were able to lend to their neighbours, and the honesty and integrity of those neighbours had a great deal to do with maintaining the credit of our people. If that honesty and integrity are destroyed, then your credit is destroyed also.
The remarks of the hon. member for Calgary West were refreshing and, I think, timely. He said some things that needed to be said. I am not so far removed from the pioneer stock. I happen to be the grandson of an old pioneer who left a comfortable home in the old country to settle in Canada. If he had been looking out for his own interests I would not be enjoying the privileges that are mine to-day. Perhaps I am reaping the benefit of that stored up labour and energy which my grandfather was prepared to sacrifice in order to accumulate, but I think that point ought to be emphasized. I will admit that I was born in the horse and buggy days, but I have seen some of the virtues of those pioneers. Let me tell my hon. friends across the way that those who have achieved success have not done so by taking advantage of some of these legalized back-door methods of practising dishonesty.

That is how I describe anything that legalizes dishonesty. It must be remembered that this measure originally was

passed in 1934, and it is not possible to correct all the errors and irregularities of society at once. I am glad the minister has taken steps to insert some provisions in the bill which will ensure a certain amount of fair play on both sides, so that the credit of the farmers may be established and the dishonest farmer may not take advantage of this measure. I do not want to be understood as saying there is any more dishonesty among farmers than among any other class; as the hon. member for Calgary West has said, farmers are as honest as any other group, but after all they are only human. I know there is the odd farmer who will put his small apples in the bottom of the basket. I have known farmers who would paint up the crack in a horse's hoof when taking it to market, or who would put a little oil on a spavined horse. There is no doubt farmers are just as astute in their own business as any other class, but in the main I think they will compare favourably with any other group of men in the country. I live in one of the smallest townships in Ontario, in which there are two hundred farmers; and in spite of all the difficulties they have had to face, in the last year they subscribed $125,000 to the victory loans. They know their business. When they want a harness they tell the harness maker just what they want, and see that they get it. He does not sell them just whatever he has hanging on the peg; they get the kind they want or they do not do business with him. That is the sort of people I represent, people who pay their debts. I am aware of only one case among those two hundred farmers in which the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act was taken advantage of, when it was in existence in Ontario.
I should like to comment for a moment on some of the homely virtues which I think we should endeavour to restore. In the early pioneer days individualism predominated, with the majesty of hard work and the glory of accomplishment.

If that remark had been made by anyone but the hon. member for Weyburn I would take it in a kindly way, but I do not think there is any hon. member of this house who has taken up more time in discussing the matters that have come up in this chamber. Personally I try not to speak unless I have something to contribute. The hon. member speaks on everything. I do not know how one man can have such a general knowledge. I would rather know one or two things well than attempt to express my opinions on a great many things and make the job of it that the hon. member does.
In regard to the payment of debts, I believe that the majesty of hard work and the glory of accomplishment still applies to this type of legislation. Sometimes I think we are wandering a long way away from that. I believe that if by accident some hon. members who have spoken were placed in a position to form a government it would be a most unfortunate thing for those people who still believe in honesty, integrity and in paying their debts.
I have other observations I should like to make in this connection, but I shall be content with making an appeal, not for that 10 per cent who go into bankruptcy through this legalized method of getting out of assuming their obligations, but for the remaining 90 per cent of the people. I have in mind the postwar period when farms will be for sale and when, if hon. members have their way, credit will have been scared away from agriculture.
I am happy to know that the minister has afforded this opportunity to the three prairie provinces to get out from under their difficulties. It would be to their advantage to accept it. I believe it was only a week or so ago I placed on record the figures supplied by the farm loan board showing payments from 1938 to 1943. Perhaps it is because we have not had the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act functioning in Ontario, but the fact remains that we have made the greatest contribution toward the payment of loans in Canada. For every dollar paid in 1938, $1.73 is being paid in 1943, and not only that, but about two and a half times as many payments are being made.
As I pointed out the other day, Alberta is not doing nearly so well. Where they paid $1 in 1938, they are paying only 84 cents to-day. One point came to my mind1 when the hon. member for Macleod was extolling to the house the virtues of the Social Credit government in Alberta. Perhaps it may be indiscreet of me to refer to the late premier of that province, but I read with interest his will, and I found that of an estate of around $33,000 only $1,500 was invested in his own repudiated bonds. It did not look very consistent, to my mind. Probably that has no bearing on this matter, but I thought it well the country should know that apparently he did not have even his own money invested in his government, of which he was premier.

I shall require only a very few minutes to say what I have to say. My experience, both as a rancher and as a farmer in western Canada, goes back over forty years. As I represent farmers and small business men, I thought I should like to say a few words on this debt bill.

Farmers' Creditors Act

I have not heard all that has been said in the debate, but one peculiar feature which has occurred to me-possibly I am wrong- is that this government bill is receiving rather less support from the government side than from the opposition side of the house. Some hon. members seem to doubt the necessity, the wisdom or even the rightness of government protection of debtors at this time. I do not know what prompted the Minister of Finance to take this action, but possibly it is the view that a healthy agriculture transcends the mere relationship between debtor and creditor, and that the very existence and future of the state depend upon a healthy and thriving agriculture.
I do not know whether this further thought has occurred to him, but it has occurred to me-and I am not blaming this government more than others-that parliament, all parliaments, are at least partly responsible for the state of affairs with which agriculture finds itself faced to-day. My mind goes back, not 1,900 years, as someone suggested the other day, but at least to the years immediately following the last war, when things were very prosperous, and the agriculturists felt justified in expanding their operations and in borrowing money for that purpose. Then, when they got things going nicely, suddenly the bottom fell out of everything. Prices went down to nothing. I have occasion to remember that, because in the winter of 1919-20, the longest on record in Alberta, either before then or since, I brought a bunch of cattle through without loss. I was quite proud of that achievement and looked forward to a worthwhile reward. But when I went to market I found that cattle which had been worth in the neighbourhood of eight cents a pound were being offered at one cent a pound. For no apparent reason-I certainly did not know the reason then-the price of cattle, and in fact all other agricultural prices, had utterly collapsed.

In the fall of 1921. I remember being in the stockyards of a small local town in which 700 head of cattle had been delivered for sale that afternoon. One cent a pound was the best price at that time.
Again in the early thirties prices were very low. I can well remember the winter of 1930-31 when eggs sold at three cents a dozen delivered. A dozen eggs would buy one bootlace. As someone said this morning, cattle did not pay for the cost of the freight, and wheat fell to twenty cents a bushel. At that time I did not have a very clear idea of the basic reasons for this collapse. I regarded

it, as now do so many hon. members of this house, as something inevitable, something in the nature of an act of God, like the weather, like a hailstorm or frost. But I have since spent the greater part of my time studying the reasons for these extraordinary differences in price levels. I know now that they are not due to natural causes, that they are artificial. In my opinion they have been deliberately brought about. I am not blaming this government any more than any other, but I do submit in all seriousness that governments and parliaments have allowed money control to get into the hands of men who are responsible to nobody but themselves, and they have manipulated it to their own great advantage. Let me read one quotation as follows:
The volume of credit in this country

In Great Britain.
7-is to a very large extent in my hands, and is related to the enterprise of the country and therefore to the encouragement or discouragement of enterprise.
And again:
Yes, I reduced credit and the purchasing of the public by 63 million pounds in the last twelve months for the reason I believe to have been sound. I am not prepared to make any suggestions how the bank could check the increase of unemployment. The bank was not unduly worried in 1925 by the possibility that the return to the pre-war gold standard would unduly interfere with British industry.
If anyone feels inclined to dispute the authority of that statement, let me say that it was made by Mr. Montagu Norman, the governor of the Bank of England, in his evidence before the Macmillan committee which I believe sat in 1930. But there is another authority, perhaps an even greater one. I quote from British Hansard of the House of Commons of April, 1932, as follows:
The price of gold has risen since then by more than 70 per cent. That is as if a 12-inch foot rule had suddenly been stretched to 19 or 20 inches; as if the pound avoirdupois had suddenly become 23 to 2! ounces instead of- how much is it?-16. Look at what this has meant to everybody who has been compelled to execute their contracts upon this irrationally enhanced scale. Look at the gross unfairness of such a distortion to all producers of new wealth, and to all that labour and science and enterprise can give us. Look at the enormously increased volume of commodities which have to be created in order to pay off the same mortgage debt or loan. Minor fluctuations might well be ignored, but I say quite seriously that this monetary convulsion has now reached a pitch where I am persuaded that the producers of new wealth will not tolerate indefinitely so hideous an oppression.
Does anyone care to question the authority or the validity of that statement? Nobody does. Those are the words of Right Hon.

Winston Churchill when he was speaking in the House of Commons as a private member in 1932. I do not know anything about agriculture in eastern Canada because I have never lived here except as a member of this house, but I do know something about farming generally in western Canada, and particularly in Alberta. I realize that this state of affairs has created a hardship not only for the debtor but also for the creditor. As the hon. member for Calgary West said, it has led to a loss of confidence as between the borrower and lender. But I do not think any good purpose is served by the creditors accusing the debtor farmers of dishonesty, incompetence or laziness. From a lifetime experience I am positive that the dishonest, incompetent and lazy farmers constitute a tiny minority. I think harm can be done by criticizing too strongly the creditors. Both sides have been victimized by a state of affairs which has no business to exist, and never would have existed if the government and parliament had exercised the right which has been vested in them.
This problem goes beyond the mere state of health of our farming industry; it affects the foundations of parliament, yes, of democracy itself. Nothing is more certain that unless parliament can bring about conditions satisfactory to the majority of the people, it will be only a question of time before the people will lose confidence in parliament. A great many people to-day have not the confidence in it they should have. Therefore I should like to impress upon hon. members as well as upon the government the absolute necessity of looking at the problem beyond the point of view of the debtor and the creditor. You can bring in temporary measures of relief for the assistance of both the creditor and the debtor, but that is not a cure; it is just a drug. I agree with the hon. member for Calgary West when he speaks of the confidence which must be restored. The confidence of the borrower must be restored if the people are to undertake to produce the wealth of this country, or the food, if you like. If they are to mortgage their future for this purpose, they must be assured of this, that if they borrow a dollar when wheat is a dollar a bushel they can repay the loan with the proceeds of one bushel of wheat, not of three or four, as the case has been in the past. Until that is done I see no remedy for the plight of the farmer. It can be done, and I say that if parliament is to endure-yes, if democracy is to endure, it must be done.

I had not intended to take part in this debate until I heard the speeches of the hon. members for Calgary West, Broadview and Brant. In
72537-324 J	.
view of the sentiments voiced by these hon. gentlemen, I feel that I must take issue with the views they have expressed.
First, however, may I compliment the minister upon the excellence of the bill which he has presented to the house. He has had a difficult task and he has done it well.
We have in the west many of the best farmers to be found anywhere. They come from all parts of Canada, from many sections of the United States, and from various countries of Europe. They left comfortable homes to pioneer and build up new homes in the west. Persons who will do that kind of thing make the best farmers and the best citizens. When they came to the prairie provinces they brought with them modern and up-to-date ideas; they discarded such methods as experience proved obsolete or undesirable, pooled their best ideas and put them into practice. I repeat that some of the best farmers to be found anywhere are in the prairie provinces.
Many of the best farmers on the prairies are most in need of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. During the last war western farmers were urged to increase their holdings and produce more in the war effort. The good, the efficient, the patriotic farmers responded to that appeal, increased their holdings and went into production on a very large scale. For this purpose they were compelled to borrow money.
During the last war there was a great deal of inflation. These farmers extended their holdings and bought stock and property of one kind and another at the height of the inflation period. When the war ended and the crash came they suffered heavy losses. Before we go through the sections one by one I think the minister ought to make a more elaborate statement than he did yesterday. In moving the second reading of the bill he gave a terse statement outlining the terms of it, but most of us expected that before the debate was concluded he would make a more general statement. I think it would help if, before we begin to go over the bill, he would make such a statement as I suggest.
Yesterday I called attention to the fact that a draft bill was presented to the government by the western debt conference. That document was contained in sessional paper 335A. Those submissions are signed by Mr. Lucien Maynard, Attorney General of Alberta, Mr. J. W. Estey, Attorney General of Saskatchewan, and Mr. Garson, Premier of Manitoba. When some hon. members, particularly the hon. member for Brant and the hon. member for Calgary West, wish to give the impression that members in this comer are trying to legalize the dishonesty by gsking for legislation that will allow some people to get out of paying their just debts, I would point out that the proposed debt legislation submitted to the government on March 15 was drawn up by responsible individuals, and two of the men who signed the submissions are prominent leaders of the Liberal party. Those submissions, therefore, ought to have been given and, I suppose, were given, some serious consideration; but no statement has been made by the minister or by any other member of the government as to why the submissions were not acceptable to the government.
As I pointed out yesterday, there are five serious omissions: (1) The transfer from the

board or tribunal to the court; (2) failure to include any clause guaranteeing the farmers' equity and making provision for the maintenance of himself and his family; (3) the insertion of a crop-failure clause in the legislation; (4) provision that there might be a revision of the board's decision from time to time; and (5) that a farmer might come within the purview of this legislation irrespective of when his debts were incurred. None of these important principles are involved in the legislation. There is involved in it something that seems to be a direct concession to the representations of the creditor class, namely, the right of appeal to the appeal courts of the three provinces.
On its face, the bill looks like an affront to the debt conference, to the three prairie provinces who participated in it and to the farmers' organizations that were-represented. I would hardly think that the minister, speaking in this case for the government, would merely wave these proposals aside without giving this committee some reason why it was impossible for the government to accept them and incorporate them in this bill. I feel that the reason why these proposals are not in the bill is that the pressure from other groups was too strong. If the minister has some good reasons why these proposals were not incorporated in this legislation, he ought to give those reasons to the committee in fairness to himself, to the committee and above all to those of that debt conference who took so much trouble to formulate the proposals and to place them before the government. The minister would help the discussion if he would tell us why those proposals were not included in the legislation now before the committee.

I think the request is a reasonable one. Three governments did join in the presentation to the government and represented that a new type of legislation should be enacted by this parliament; I mean new in the sense that it had never been enacted in any province of the dominion, or in the Dominion of Canada or, so far as I can find, in any other country in the world. The main new feature was this, that instead of recognizing the emergency aspect of the debt situation in western Canada and framing legislation with a view to meeting that temporary emergency, it was proposed for the first time that the boards to be set up, which would continue to function through the years, should deal with debts whether incurred in the past or to be incurred in the future, and that these boards would have the power to write down debts without obliging the debtor to divest himself of his assets. That is a right which no other person in the Dominion of Canada has. It is
a right which the farmers of eastern Canada do not want. It is a right which business in eastern Canada would not ask for. And as to its being an affront to the western governments and the western debt conference, my only answer is this, that this government must take its responsibility and this parliament must take its responsibility for enacting legislation of a type which they can defend and for what they can answer to the electors.
Bear in mind that the main feature, the startling feature, of the proposal which came from the debt conference in western Canada was this, that instead of proceeding on the principle which underlay the debt adjustment acts of all the provinces, which had a date limit in them, a date limit which was moved, I believe, in three acts, perhaps under pressure-I do not know-instead of having a date limit and regarding this extraordinary legislation as being emergency legislation to meet a temporary situation, the western governments for the first time requested this government to do something which none of them had ever done, and that was to set up open-ended legislation which would allow debt adjustment boards to sit for all time to come and whittle down and reduce the debts through the years and decades and centuries regardless of whether there was any emergency or not.
When that proposal was presented to me I took a very serious view of it, and I can assure hon. gentlemen that I did not communicate with the mortgage companies or with any lending institution. I simply searched in my own mind for some principles by which to test it.

speechtext: Did they communicate with the minister?

Not then. Later they did. I gave them an opportunity to make representations, and I told the representatives of western Canada that I was going to give them an opportunity of making representations.
I searched in my own mind for some principles to go on. I think the fundamental difference between the two types of legislation that are contended for in this house, the fundamental difference of view is this: Is farm credit worth preserving or not? There are some people who think it is not. I have had persons who in talking to me said it was not, that it did not make much difference whether the farmer could borrow money from private lenders in the future, that credit had been bad for him in the past, and that he does not need credit, should' not have credit, but should be obliged to pay cash for the land and other things he wants to buy. But no one in this debate- and I have heard a wide variety of opinions
Farmers' Creditors Act

expressed and all schools of thought here- not even the wildest-eyed speaker, has gone to the length of saying that the farmer should be deprived of his credit standing. But I am satisfied that if we were to set up boards and let it be known that we were setting up boards which would have the power of reducing debts at their own discretion, regardless of the security taken, regardless of the ability of the debtor to pay -if we were to do that, people would not lend farmers money at all. Why should they? I have had some arguments about that. ^ I have said: Well, perhaps they would size the farmer up and say that man is a good fellow, an honest man who will pay if he can on account of his moral qualities. If he has high moral qualities, some people would take a chance on him. Some individuals might lend him money, but certainly no trust funds would be lent under a law like that.

speechtext: Was not one of the principles in the draft bill that the farmer's ability to pay should be taken into consideration in 'making adjustments?

speechtext:
Yes, certainly, it should be taken into consideration, but bear in mind what the lender is lending on-not on the security of property, as in the past. In the past he has been assured that if the value were there the value would be pledged to the extent of his security. But he is lending, not upon property, but upon the discretion of a board, upon what the board thinks about it. He naturally does not know what kind of members will be appointed to the boards through the years. Perhaps you could get a high calibre of board; perhaps you could not. There is a tremendous difference in the judgment of the members of these boards, and the result is that he would not have any solidity to his security.
If hon. gentlemen think, and they may, that is not a worth-while objective to strive for, to preserve a system under which there will be some credit extended on the security of land; if they do not think that is worth while, I do not know that I have a great deal of fault to find with their position. Perhaps they would set up some system whereby the state would lend money. I am sure that if that system were set up many bad loans would be made under the pressure of agitators. Nevertheless they may think that is a better system. But I frankly say-it may be background or the way I was brought up or something like that-I believe that people should pay their debts if they can. I believe that when they sign a note or sign a mortgage the

security they give should be applied to the satisfaction of the first charge on the property. That is what I think should be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
You have no idea how many questions I have been wanting to ask and refrained from asking.
There are two possible principles of any legislation that could be introduced into this house. One principle is this, that you should set up a board that would do a thing which has not been done by anybody else, which was never done by any province, which was never done by the dominion, and never done, I believe, by any other country, and that this continuing court, for that is what it would be, would place the security of creditors at the mercy of boards so that a creditor would never know whether you could apply his full security to the satisfaction of his debt or not, but would have to rely on the discretion of the board as to whether his full security could be applied for the satisfaction of his debt-and that to go on throughout the years continuously. The other principle is this, whether you should confine the character of this legislation to what it was in the beginning, emergency legislation.
We stuck to the original principle of this bill. It is based on the theory that in the twenties, probably in the teens before, when there was a great demand for land in western Canada, and when very high prices were paid for land in western Canada, higher prices than the farmers could pay as subsequent developments showed, these mortgages were put on and these agreements for sale were outstanding. Then, when the thirties came along it was discovered that the farmers simply could not get out of debt, so that something had to be done.

Farmers' Creditors Act
Under the old legislation only the debts that existed before May 1, 1935, could be adjusted ; no debts incurred after that date could be dealt with by the board, except by consent. That was very unsatisfactory. It meant that a farmer would go before a board of review and that part of his debts could be adjusted1, while part could not. We changed that and said that if two-thirds of his debts were incurred before May 1, 1935, then all his debts could be adjusted up to date, whenever they were incurred.
That is one thing we have done. We might have left it there, but we realized that there was a great deal of inconsistency in the treatment individual farmers received at the hands of these boards of review in the years 1935, 1936 and 1937. I think those were the years when there was the greatest difference in the treatment, as compared with subsequent years. Up to about the end of 1937 they did not get very many concessions from the boards of review, but were debarred from making a second application. As a result, some of those people are still weighed down with those old debts, so that by this legislation we have allowed them to come in again and make a second proposal. That applies to those whose compositions were made not later than the end of 1938. We gave a great deal of consideration to the date we should fix, and we thought December 31, 1938, was late enough. We had considered for a while making it the middle of 1937, but we thought we would err on the other side and bring it down to the end of 1938. Mind you, the creditor cannot reopen the matter, but the debtor can. When I hear hon. gentlemen talking about this legislation having the mark of a surrender to the mortgage companies, I can point out feature after feature of this legislation certainly not in the interests of the mortgage companies, narrowly considered. I wish to say that the mortgage companies are not suited with this legislation. They never saw it before last Saturday, and their reaction to it has been anything but favourable. However, I think the legislation is reasonably just, if we accept the principle that this is emergency legislation and not continuing legislation to meet both past and future debts. I do not see how we could justify that; I do not think it would pass this house and, if it did pass this house, there are other places I do not think it would pass.
Let me mention some of the features that are unfavourable to the companies. It must be great political stuff in -western Canada to talk about these companies; I never realized that it was such good political material until
yesterday. Here is the hon. member for Acadia, for whom I have a great deal of respect and who argues in a fairly consecutive sort of way in this house, particularly on financial matters. Yesterday he could not help calling the mortgage companies bloodsuckers. Well, Mr. Chairman, what is this forum? Is it a place for the discussion of principles, or is it a place for making political speeches? I do not have any brief for the mortgage companies, certainly, but I do not believe in the abuse of any class of Canadian citizens or Canadian institutions. I want to say this, and it was brought out by the hon. member for Calgary West. It must be remembered that the insurance companies, which are the heavy lenders on these mortgages, are the trustees of the savings of the people. There are millions of small policyholders in this country, and the money these insurance companies are putting out is the money of these policyholders. That is all brushed aside, however, as though the policyholders were in the bloodsucker class too; as though they were not worthy of consideration, and as though the ordinary principles of British justice should not apply to those people because they are not western farmers. I must express my dissent from that sort of approach to the discussion of these questions. We must tiy to work out something here which will be fair and just, which will recognize that all classes of individuals and institutions in this country have certain elementary rights based on what we call British justice.
Let me point out some of the features of this legislation. Had we been trying to please the mortgage companies, certainly we would not have provided for the reopening of those cases which were adjudicated between 1935 and the end of 1938, and certainly we would not have provided that the farmer could reopen them while the company could not. We would not have inserted the section about appeals, to provide that the companies cannot possibly recover any costs on appeal, except where the debtor brought a clearly unreasonable appeal. We were very careful in drafting the section on appeals to make it as far as possible a section which would not favour the wealthy litigant, or the litigant who had funds with which to carry on his appeal.
This legislation must be taken in conjunction with the order in council which, as the hon. member for Swift Current pointed out, is an integral, essential and most important feature of the debt legislation of this parliament, passed under the War Measures Act. That order in council, which we intend to continue
Farmers' Creditors Act

for the duration of the war, carries out the essential provisions of the Saskatchewan debt adjustment legislation, which in proper cases enables debtors to secure postponement of foreclosure proceedings which would put them off the land. That must be taken in conjunction with this legislation. We have transferred this matter to the courts. I have not very much to say about that. I agree with what the hon. member for Peace River said yesterday about the courts as compared with the boards of review. I do not know that I would put it just on the grounds he did, that the courts will work for the debtor to a greater extent than the boards did, but I think the courts are a better forum than the board. We have had these boards now since 1935. I have been the minister responsible for their operation and I never knew what control I had or did not have over the boards. They were judicial, but not wholly so. They were administrative boards, and it seemed to be assumed by a great many persons in the country that if they got what they considered a raw deal at the hands of these boards, they could appeal to the minister, who could step in and change it just as he would be able to overrule an administrative official. I never knew whether I could or could not do that. These boards were headed by supreme court judges of the'provinces, and there was always pressure of this kind and the other to appoint a man of this type or of that type to the board, so that he might give this type of decision or that type of decision. Of course the government has to take that responsibility, but it is disagreeable to have to make choices of that kind all the time, between this suggested appointee and the other. Now there is no doubt that the operation of this measure is not in any way under the control of the minister. It is within the courts; it is a wholly judicial procedure. We have tried in this measure to lay down principles for the guidance of the courts, as far as that could be done; but, once we have done that; once we have made -the best possible selection of appellate judges, the legislation will have to take its course, and I think that is a very much more satisfactory way to have it.
I do not believe there should be the power for debtors to get adjustment after adjustment. There must be some finality in this matter. That is a different subject from the one I mentioned before, the power to come in with future debts. But it seems to me that one adjustment is enough. It seems to me that if we were to go on the principle that there are to be repeated adjustments, then repeated adjustment in favour of the creditor would have to be granted, too. We did not do that for the period between 1935

and 1938. We made it one way, because the whole aot is based upon proposals by the farmer. But if we were to allow or to lay down the general principle that the farmer can go time after time for adjustments, it seems to me only fair that the creditor could do it, too. And that would not be good for the farmer, let me tell you.
There are some features in this measure with which I shall deal as the sections are reached. But I must point out that great care has been used in the drafting of it. I am satisfied that this is as far as we could go. I do not agree with the extremists, who have expressed their views either on one side or the other in this debate. I think something should be done to lift this load of old debt which proved too heavy to enable the farmer to cope with the adversities of the thirties. I think something should be done to enable those situations to be dealt with, and that emergency to be cleared up. In other words, I think we should stick to the emergency character of the legislation, and stick to the essential principle of the legislation; but we should keep it so that it will be more workable. We have made a number of changes to overcome the result of decisions by courts which have been in favour of the creditors. That will be seen, as we go through the sections of the bill.
There are a number of remedies of that kind. I must repudiate the idea that we have been dictated to or that to any considerable extent we have been influenced by either one faction or the other in this matter.
No one could listen to the speeches in the house without seeing at once the wide variety of opinions held, even among ourselves. And that wide variety of opinion exists throughout the country. Certain hon. members have read letters from farmers who have had a hard time. Well, I could read letters from women, widows, who have sold farms and taken mortgages, and then been taken in before the boards and had their mortgages cut away down by boards of review under conditions which, to my mind, would appear entirely unjust.
I believe that what the hon. member for Calgary West has said is true. This is legislation of a continuing character, and applying to most debts. But I believe it can be said truly that a man in his advancing years will rent his farm to a young man rather than sell it. That is the condition, unless that man can get practically the full cash price. In other words, I think it hurts credit, and it would be a bad thing to adopt legislation on any different principle.

One fundamental principle has
been entirely ignored. I believe we have every justification for asking that these appeals be of a recurrent nature. I have particular reference to prices for farm production. Looking back over the years I can remember wheat at $3.60 a bushel, and I also know of some farms which were bought in those days. Then, looking ahead twelve or thirteen years later than the period I have mentioned,
I remember wheat selling for twenty cents a bushel in western Canada. To-day we have no assurance of any guaranteed price for wheat. Until that is guaranteed, or until some provision is made under which the products of the farm can be sold at a profit, then I say the farmers are entitled to the protection for which they have asked through the medium of appeals from time to time for the adjustment of their debts.

speechtext:
I believe the minister
thought I had been somewhat extravagant in one of the terms I have used. But he must remember this, that I lived on the edge of the drouth area. I have seen the farmers who came to that area, and lived on those farms for perhaps twenty years. Then I have seen them driven off their farms by the mortgage companies. The treatment they have received in the past has been merciless. I fancy that if the minister had seen what I have seen out there, he would probably appreciate the reason why I used those terms. That is why in the past provincial governments were forced to take action. They had to take action to prevent that sort of thing from taking place. I have heard it said that interest rates are high on account of the type of the debt legislation, and the manner in which it operates. But those high rates of interest were in existence long before debt legislation was introduced in 1907, 1908 or 1909.

speechtext: What about the risk?

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The hon. member refers .to risk. I say that when you obtain a high rate of interest you must not squeal when you lose. You are charging that high rate of interest in order to take care of your risk. Those mortgage companies were charging 8, 9, 10 and even 12 per cent in those days, and if they lost something on their investment they certainly had no right to squeal, because they were getting their high rate of interest. If the mortgage companies had been prepared to lend money at 4J or 5 per cent, I would have agreed that they perhaps should have had better security. But any concern which considers
itself justified in charging 10 or 12 per cent interest had no right whatsoever to squeal if it lost on its investment. That is all part of the game, and part of the gamble.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the section is passed, I believe it would be well to say a word or two with respect to this measure, perhaps by way of summing up. I listened to the words of the hon. member for Calgary West. He took the orthodox stand of those who must protect credit, just as the minister did. I think the minister will find there is no hon. member in my party, or perhaps in any other party in the house, who does not agree that there must be a protection of credit. I believe that would be accepted by everybody. The difficulty lies, however, in taking the whole thing out of the farmer.
It has been brought out several times by various speakers to-day and yesterday that there is an extremely unsatisfactory agricultural policy in Canada. The debt situation is largely the result of that policy. And we are looking to debt legislation to adjust or to make amends for the flaws produced by or the evils resulting from that agricultural policy.
I shall spend only a moment or two in a discussion of that policy. I have referred to it once before, in the discussion with respect to wool. I do not propose to repeat what I said on that occasion, but somehow or another the minister has to have somebody teach him that there is something radically wrong with the whole agricultural policy of Canada. And if someone does not get it into the minister's head, then I am telling him that he is going to wreck the country. It will be altogether too late to talk about it, when the thmg is accomplished. I shall point out briefly to the minister the chief flaws in the agricultural policy of Canada.
In the first place there simply must be a scaling down of agricultural debt. I am not in favour of mortgage companies losing their money. I am not in favour of seeing lenders lose their money. But what are we to do? Obviously, the sensible thing is not to let the farmers be ruined on the land. What is to be done? I am informed that in the United States and in New Zealand they are adopting a systematic, comprehensive scheme of scaling down debts. Just how that should be done will cause some doubt, but I believe that ultimately the Dominion of Canada will have to step in as a nation and absorb the shock. If the Dominion of Canada, as the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) suggested yesterday, allowed men by the tens of thousands to come in and settle in the Palliser triangle
Farmers' Creditors Act

and then, when those men have accumulated debts, washes its hands of responsibility in the matter, then obviously the Dominion of Canada is failing in its responsibility to the people it had brought into the country.
What is to be done about it? Suppose a man comes into the country, as I have seen men do, with $20,000 and invests that money in a piece of land in the Palliser triangle after there have been years of good crops and without knowing how uncertain the weather is in that area; what is to happen when he has four or five bad years and his debts accumulate and become unpayable as they inevitably will? What would the minister's stand be in connection with that man who has brought $20,000 into the country to invest along with five, six or seven years of his life? Must that man lose everything? Is that the stand the minister takes? If it is, then he is taking a most extravagant stand, one more extravagant by far than that taken by the hon. member for Acadia.
The question the minister will immediately ask the member for Lethbridge is, "Should the person who lends that man another $20,000 on his land lose his money?" My answer would be that it is not right that either of them should lose his money. But certain it is that the man who came into the country with $20,000 and invested it in a piece of Canadian land has a right which this country ought to protect. If it does not protect that right, then the government is destroying the credit of the country in another way. If the minister asks where he is going now with his agricultural policy, let me say that the time may come when they will nretty nearly have to hire men to go farming on the land.

speechtext:
I would say that perhaps there is a little difference between a mining venture and an agricultural venture. Nevertheless I believe the time is rapidly coming when men are beginning to argue that the government should guarantee them protection before they put their money even into a mine. That is being done at the present time. The government has already found it necessary to guarantee loans for the development of mines, to pay for the development of mines and to allow concessions in taxation. The government has had to resort to a great many expedients to encourage private capital to go into industry. Farming is an industry, and the government 
must do something like that to guarantee a man his security in farming. I doubt very much if in 1935 Liberals would have favoured the creation of as many crown companies as the Liberal government has established in Canada to-day. I doubt very much if in 1935 the Minister of Finance would have favoured the various advances of money which have been made by the dominion government to different companies to encourage them to produce war needs. A new concept has grown up with the years. The new policy is the result of the new concept. The new policy when applied to farming will result in an altogether different way of treating the farmer. I wonder if the Minister of Mines and Resources is answered; does the minister feel that his question has been answered?

I believe it is
answered. If it is not, the minister can ask me another. The point is that we have reached the place where we must realize that in order to secure the state we must do things which have not been done before. The United States has found it necessary to scale down debts, and I would not be surprised if the United States treasury has reimbursed those who have lost in the scaling down. I would not be surprised if the Dominion of Canada should find it necessary to do a similar thing. I am not in favour of having the mortgage companies lose their money. I am not in favour of the people who have placed their savings with the life insurance companies losing their money. No member of the Alberta legislature or of this Social Credit party would favour that. I doubt if there is one member of the party who could be found to subscribe to that view.
What Social Crediters found in Alberta was an impossible situation. They found that the claims of the money-lenders and the claims of the human element were in conflict, and as a result of that conflict the human element was toeing destroyed, just as the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Ross) so well said. I think he did his province a service this afternoon. He is a man Who has come in contact with reality. I am not saying that the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Edwards) was extreme in his views because he

Farmers' Creditors Act
represented one point of view. But the hon. member for Calgary East showed quite clearly that he realized there was another point of view, and that the two points of view must be reconciled. How to reconcile them is the problem. The only way they can be reconciled as far as I can see is to have a scaling down of debt. This will involve the advance of money from the dominion treasury to reimburse in some measure those who may be caused to lose money.
