subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Just before the
committee took recess I was discussing the faults in the agricultural policy as it is at present applied in Canada, and pointing out to the minister that one reason why we encounter so much difficulty in drafting a bill of this sort is that we are trying through the bill to rectify abuses which develop naturally through a faulty agricultural policy in the country, and I said that it would become necessary, in order to adjust the onerous debt situation which has developed in western Canada, for the dominion government to step into the picture and absorb the shock, actually reimbursing in considerable measure those who have lent the money, and also reimbursing in considerable measure those who have borrowed, to overcome a situation which is otherwise intolerable.
So that the stand of the Social Credit party may be made completely clear on this matter, and for the minister's use, I am going to read a passage from a booklet recently published and issued from Edmonton just prior to Premier Aberhart's death. This little booklet is called "Prepare Now: A Suggested Policy for Post-War Reconstruction". On page 43 of this booklet I read as follows:
All agricultural mortgage debts to be taken over by an agricultural credit bank operating under the national monetary authority, on the following basis:
(a)	The principal amount of debts to be reduced to the original indebtedness less all payments made in excess of three per cent. The farmer will be required to pay this to the agricultural credit bank in equitable instalments on a crop or production share basis.
(b)	The agricultural credit bank will repay creditors on equitable terms which will ensure that individuals incur no loss and corporations can meet their liabilities in full.
I propose to deal briefly with what is suggested there, elaborating in some measure. It will be noticed that the principle laid
down is that the interest rate should not exceed three per cent. I believe the minister in his bill and in the operation of the bill should have in mind the idea that the interest rate should not exceed three per cent. We have heard mention made of exorbitant rates such as eight, nine, ten and eleven per cent. All such rates are deleterious to the country and will result in hardship and destruction of our vital resources. If the original loan to a given farmer is allowed to stand and the lender allowed interest at the rate of three per cent from the time when the money was lent, and the debt is taken over by the agricultural credit bank and provision made that the lender shall receive his principal with interest at the rate of three per cent, the lender, I think we shall agree, will not suffer seriously by such an arrangement and the farmer will be required to pay this to the agricultural credit bank in equitable instalments on a crop or production share basis. We have found in Alberta that a satisfactory way of dealing with agricultural debt is to allow the farmer to pay a certain portion of his crop each year. If he does this, he does not have the anxiety of having to sell the crop, turn it into money and pay the money. The person to whom the money is owed knows he is getting a certain percentage of the crop, and he knows that is fair; he feels much better about it, and the farmer feels much better about it. The first thing you know, the debt is beginning to be liquidated. This principle is suggested in what I have read. It goes on to state:
The agricultural credit bank will repay creditors on equitable terms which will ensure that individuals incur no loss. . . .
The hon. member for Calgary West, with an arrangement like that being worked out, would have no cause to worry about the money which had been put into life insurance companies. Any life insurance company which had lent money to a farmer would be guaranteed the money it lent him together with three per cent interest, which would certainly enable the company to discharge the obligations to the people who had insured their lives with it. Probably that little passage will help members of the committee to understand what I meant when I said that the government would step in and reimburse, not necessarily permanently, probably just temporarily-for twenty years or so, the idea being that ultimately the government would recover its money, the farmers would get out of debt, the people who lent money to
Farmers' Creditors Act

the farmers would get their money back, and the country would be restored to a sound, healthy condition with respect to debt.
I mentioned a minute ggo the question of refunding. I see no reason why the minister should not adopt the policy of refunding to enable farmers to borrow at low rates of interest the money with which to discharge their obligations over a long period of time, say twenty or thirty years, which would enable them to get out from under their indebtedness and would enable the people who have lent money to the farmers to recover their money without too much hardship and inconvenience.
The matter of price must be taken care of, and the minister has not made allowance for that in drafting the bill. As the hon. member for Battle River pointed out, prices simply must be guaranteed from year to year, so that farmers will know where they stand and the people who are lending the money will know where they stand; otherwise the credit which the minister was so anxious about will be lost. If the lending companies come to find by and by that, no matter how good a farmer a man may be, if they lend money to him and prices go down they lose their money, they will certainly lose confidence and the country will lose credit in spite of such legislation as this. There can be no question about it. So that this bill will not protect the credit of the country, even though the minister believes it will.
Just to show the minister that prices in Canada are not where they ought to be, may I quote briefly from a statement made at Brandon, Manitoba, on June 24, and reported by the Canadian Press:
William Bryce, of Dugald, Manitoba, urged the cost of production plus ten per cent for farmers, the same as industry, in his presidential address to the Manitoba Federation of Agriculture meeting here yesterday.
Farmers all over the country are beginning to talk about being paid on a cost-plus basis rather than on a cost-minus basis as they are being paid at the present time. May I tell the minister that no matter how carefully he drafts this bill, unless he looks after the matter of price in the agricultural economy of this country he cannot possibly sustain the credit of the farmer.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Will the hon. member tell
us how he would establish cost of production on the farm?

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The hon. member
has asked a pertinent question. I would say that probably in Canada the thing to do would be to start with wheat. I fancy our whole agricultural economy is built around
[Mr. Blackmore.J
wheat. The cost of wheat, the price at which it ought to be sold, could be determined, I believe, by a group of experts similar to those now working on the wartime prices and trade board. Three years ago a good many things which now look thoroughly feasible would have seemed impossible, and I think the hon. member for Maple Creek will agree with me that a group of men such as Donald Gordon has in his employ could determine after a while the price at which wheat should be sold.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: It might be pretty cheap.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
It should not be
cheap. If they determined a price for wheat which was cheap they would be cheap themselves, because the whole country would be based upon a cheap economy. In fact, that is the trouble with us now. The price of wheat, I should say, should be between $1.25 and $1.50 if it were set where it ought to be to enable the farmers to carry on year after year and to build fences when they break down and barns when they are worn out. Then, having wheat as the pivotal point, they could set for other primary products like barley, oats, rye and other commodities, such prices as would enable the growers to produce those commodities as economically as they could produce wheat. Does that indicate to the hon. member how he ought to proceed? This could be done with regard to all the various agricultural commodities. A fair price could be determined for them. In a general way this ideal should obtain. The object should be, in the economy of any country, to enable the people on the farms to buy from industry the products they need and to enable those engaged in industry to buy from the farms their own requirements. With that general idea in mind, and with the technique I have indicated, I am sure that any group of experts who went to work seriously on the problem could determine fair and profitable prices for all primary products, and then arrive at the prices of the secondary commodities by a similar device. I am not discussing that matter to-night, but I have shown in a general way how one could proceed.
I believe there are just two other matters the minister should bear in mind. First of all, he should see to it that the farmers get credit where they need it, the credit which they cannot now obtain; and he should make ample provision for stability of prices and of markets for the next three years. If he would do that, there would not be very much difficulty about the bill he has introduced. I am not sure that there would be great objection to it in

Farmers' Creditors Act
its present form if the inequalities and injustices that are inherent in the whole agricultural economy were removed.
I believe that the hon. member for Acadia took a sound position. He said that the bill was deficient in at least three respects, in a general way. First, the boards are done away with and courts substituted. Although there is disagreement among the members regarding the desirability of boards as compared with courts, in my opinion the boards have done very good work. We found in Alberta that there was not much complaint on the part of the farmers with reference to the work of the boards, and I am not sure that the loan companies suffered much at their hands. I believe also, as the hon. member for Battle River has emphasized two or three times, that the debt situation must be dealt with on the basis of its being recurrent. In southern Alberta, south of Calgary, there is drouth this year. The hon. member for Medicine Hat the other day brought this fact to the attention of the house. That drouth will cost hundreds of thousands of dollars to farmers all over that country. The farmers are not responsible for it; there is nothing they can do about it. The farmer put in his grain in perfectly good faith, but he will not have anything to live on this year, or at any rate very little, and debts will accumulate. Even the Minister of Finance, with his orthodox mind, would hardly blame -the farmer for the debts that- will accumulate in consequence of what has happened this year through an act of God. It is that very thing that creates the situation for which there must be a remedy, some means of absorbing the shock. To go to that part of the country and tell the farmers that they should absorb the whole shock of that terrible drouth from Calgary south, is to make oneself ridiculous. The minister sees, I believe, that what the farmers are suffering from all over the three western provinces is a long period of years in which incidents similar to this drouth have impaired the economic stability of the farmers and thrown them into debt. The debt situation therefore must be dealt with as a recurrent problem; and when the minister says that he does not believe there should be more than one or two decisions on the debt question, I reply that he is out of contact with realities. In fact, he made the statement that there was to be only one proposal. Well, one is not enough. Hundreds of farmers in southern Alberta alone this year will have to have a readjustment from the adjustment they made last year. How else will they meet the situation which will
develop as a result of the drouth which destroys their crop? Surely the debt situation must be dealt with as a recurring problem.
There is injustice also in requiring that the debt should be such that two-thirds of it had been contracted prior to May 1, 1935. From what I have said I think it must be clear that the question of debt is one that is likely to come up at any time. The terrible hail storms that sometimes sweep across that section of the country will put the farmers in a position where they cannot discharge their obligations. If they contracted debts when the stores gave them credit, how will they discharge those debts if next year there is frost or a drouth? How will they adjust themselves? We have had many experiences of that kind in Alberta, and therefore we know that some of the things the minister has said are more or less doctrinaire and are not the result of facing realities.
I would say that there are three main flaws in the bill which should be remedied to bring it up to that standard which would be thoroughly acceptable to the people in- the west.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: This bill is for the purpose of facilitating compromises and arrangements between insolvent farmers and their creditors. But is it possible to do anything for those who are insolvent, or is the definition of the word "insolvent" to be extended and given such a wide interpretation as to take in those who merely want readjustment of their debts?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: They must be unable to meet their debts as they fall due; otherwise they do not come under the legislation, We would not have the jurisdiction to deal with the others, because the basis of our jurisdiction is that section in the British North America Act which gives this parliament jurisdiction over bankruptcy and insolvency.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
In the draft bill presented by the debt conference there were one or two things which were asked for, which seemed to be basic but which apparently have been entirely neglected in the bill before us. In paragraph 15 they point out particularly that they want the boards to protect the farmer's interest, to evaluate the farmer's interest in the farm land as represented by the amount of money, principal and interest, which he had paid, and, second, the amount of cultivation and improvements he had made and the labour he had expended in bringing the lands into an improved condition. That is one thing I wish to bring to the minister's attention.
farmers' Creditors Act

Another point is this. In protecting the farmer's interests they want to base the adjustment on the ability of the debtor to pay, and I believe that has been taken care of. They say in paragraph 15 (3):
15. In exercising its jurisdiction and powers to formulate a plan of settlement and without limiting its discretion in any way the board may consider and determine inter alia the following matters:
(3) The cost of maintenance of the debtor and his family at a reasonable standard of living and the current expenditures reasonably necessary in the operation of his farm.
I think that is fundamental, and if this bill is to be an effective instrument, those things should be taken into consideration. A number of the other proposals made have been incorporated in the bill.
The minister this afternoon argued that if revisions or adjustments as asked for by the debt conference were provided for, it would destroy farm credit and cause tenantry in this country. I would point out to the minister that when agriculture or any other industry suffers the losses which were suffered by the farmers of the west whom this bill is supposed to protect, someone has to take the losses, and where such loss is suffered credit is bound to be destroyed, and to accept this proposal would not prevent that.
As regards tenantry, the records show that it is increasing rapidly in the west, and the reason why it has increased more rapidly over the past few years is that it has not paid the creditor to foreclose on the farm because he could not go in himself and operate the land and make any more profit out of it than the farmer did. About eighty per cent of the farms of my province are already mortgaged, and if prosperous times should ever come to agriculture again, there would be so many foreclosures that tenantry would be widespread.	,

speechtext: Paragraph (h) defines " farmer." We have a great many ranchers in Alberta who, I submit, should have the benefit of the act. I presume the minister would have no objection to an amendment making the definition broad enough to include ranchers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I just followed the timehonoured language which is used in the Bankruptcy Act and in the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. I do not think I would like to broaden the definition.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I think the definition of "farmer" should be broadened to include men who, while not actually residing on the farm, are operating the farm and making it their chief occupation. They pay all the expenses and taxes and hire the labour for the farm. I think that class should be included in the definition.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I would ask the
minister whether the definition of "farmer" as it now stands would cover a person who had

Farmers' Creditors Act
been engaged in farming but is now retired from the farm and relies mainly upon his returns from the farm for his support. Personally I think the definition, as was pointed out by the two hon. members who have just referred to it, is not sufficiently wide to cover the various situations that have been found to arise since the definition was first incorporated in the original act. I would suggest to the minister that ranchers be included within the ambit of the expression " farmer." There are many who are engaged in ranching, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Calgary East, who, I believe, are entitled to be included under the act but have been excluded under the judgments to which he made reference. subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I wish to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary East in regard to the definition of "farmer". I think it was found necessary, either under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act or the wheat acreage reduction scheme, to change the definition of the word "farmer" so that ranchers would be included. I believe a rancher was defined as a man with so many head of stock per acre, or on some similar basis, and I believe the minister will find that this definition must also be changed. There will be a great deal of dissatisfaction if it is left to include only those whose main occupation is farming or the tillage of the soil. I believe some qualification will have to be made so that ranchers will be included, perhaps so many head of stock for each acre of land or something like that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: What is the case for bringing ranchers under the legislation? My hon. friend assumes that ranchers should come under it, but what is the case for making it apply to ranchers? The great complaint from ranchers recently has been in connection with the excess profits tax.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The situation is quite clear in some districts, particularly in the southern parts of the prairie provinces. You may find the case of a man who has been farming and who has changed over to
ranching. If a farmer is in that position, he has every right to come under this legislation. Of course, if you are going to have it apply only to those who are bankrupt now, instead of making it a debt adjustment act, this definition may be all right, for those who are going to be sold out will be sold out anyway. If it is to be a debt reduction act, however, to assist these ranchers and farmers, the definition must be widened to meet the case.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: It all depends upon how you define a "farmer" and a "rancher". As the hon. member for Bow River says, under the Wheat Acreage Reduction Act anyone with more than fifty head of stock, or more than two head of stock for every acre of wheat, was called a rancher. The minister is not going to suggest that a farmer with fifty-five head of cattle will be very much worried about the excess profits tax. During the years from 1932 on, when stock was selling for as low as a dollar a head, many of these small ranchers got into serious financial difficulty, and it will take a number of years for them to get back on their feet. When we come to section 7 I intend to refer to a point which will very much affect the ranchers; that is, in connection with the deadline of 1935. The ranchers who had to sell off their stock in 1937, in order to become eligible for feed under the dominion regulations, certainly need help to-day. Many of those ranchers were out of debt in 1935; then when the drouth hit them they had to sell most of their stock and take whatever they could get for them. Now they get no consideration at all under this measure. However, that will come up when we reach section 7. I am only pointing out now that many ranchers have suffered heavy financial losses, and certainly I think at least the small rancher should come under this legislation. I believe the minister was referring to what one might call the business rancher or the syndicate rancher, but under the provisions of the Wheat Acreage Reduction Act a farmer with over fifty head of stock is called a rancher.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: It seems that the courts of Alberta have decided that a rancher is not a farmer within the meaning of this measure.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: How is a rancher defined?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I do not know. I did not know the courts had made that finding, but I have the word of the hon. member for Calgary East for it, and that is confirmed by the official in charge. Certainly the definition in thp wheat acreage reduction regulations would have no bearing at all on the case. I am not familiar with the decisions of the courts of Alberta, but this measure is designed to assist
Farmers' Creditors Act

persons whose principal occupation is farming or the tillage of the soil. I do not know the difference between farming and the tillage of the soil; I questioned that when I was going over the bill, but I was informed that this language had been interpreted by the courts, that it is the language of the old Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and that it is the language of the Bankruptcy Act. subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
What is that definition
again?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS

Mr. ILSLEY; Under this legislation a person whose principal occupation was not farming or the tillage of the soil would not be eligible for the benefits of the legislation. He would be regarded as a person in a different kind of business, and why not? It is just a question of where the line should be drawn. We cannot extend this measure to include everybody; it has just applied to those whose principal occupation consisted in farming or the tillage of the soil.

Then I think the measure should definite the difference between a rancher and a farmer. We ran into that problem with the Wheat Acreage Reduction Ac't. Many farmers were denied the bonus on the ground that they were ranchers; finally the Minister of Agriculture stated that the regulation was ridiculous, and he wiped it out. Now ranchers are eligible for the wheat acreage reduction bonus. If a rancher can be

eligible for the wheat acreage reduction bonus, he must be a tiller of the soil; therefore he should come under this legislation.

They do a certain amount of farming; they grow coarse grains for their cattle, but 'their chief occupation is ranching and not tilling of the soil. speechtext:
I have particular
reference to subsection 3 of this section which I believe is not properly worded, in that in line 24 the word "may" appears. I think it should read "shall," for the following reasons. The section as it now stands reads as follows:
If the court is satisfied that a member of the family of the decedent or of such farmer resides and will continue to reside on the farm of the decedent or of such farmer, who intends and is able to operate the same, the court may, ex parte . . . grant such application.
The section as it now stands with the permissive "may" therein will, I submit, hold out hopes that farmers who live on the land following the death of the owner would have the right and the opportunity to come under the provisions of this bill. The use of the word "may," being permissive, means that a discretionary order will be made which will, if the ordinary rules are followed, not be altered on appeal. As the bill is drawn, I think the result will be that a land court jurisprudence will be established, and we shall find ourselves in the position that each district court judge will determine applications from the sons and daughters of deceased farmers according to his own whims and wishes. Provision for appeals is to be found in section 24, which provides:
An appeal may be taken from any judgment or order of the court made in any proceedings under this act pursuant to a proposal, including an order approving or confirming a composition, extension of time or scheme of arrangement or declining to formulate a proposal, to the appeal court in the province in which the court has jurisdiction, and shall be asserted, heard and decided according to the ordinary procedure governing appeals from judgments or orders of the court to the court of appeal in such province, subject to any special rules of practice and procedure relating thereto made under this act.
The ordinary rule is that a discretionary order is not reversed on appeal. The fact that the district court judge may make an order shows that the order he may make will be discretionary; and where he refuses the right to the sons or daughters, as the case may be, of a deceased farmer, their right will not be altered on appeal in view of the fact that the ordinary principles of Jaw will apply. I suggest to the minister that the right should be absolute; that where a member of the family of the deceased will continue on the farm, and intends and is able to operate the same, he
Farmers' Creditors Act

should enjoy the right to apply under this bill. Therefore I suggest for the minister's consideration that the permissive word "may" be deleted and the mandatory "shall" substituted therefor.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I should like to ask a question with respect to the powers

Farmers' Creditors Act

of the board. Again, it seems to me, the phraseology is quite vague. The section states:
On the written request of a creditor or of the farmer, where the official receiver reports that the farmer has made a proposal but that no proposal has been approved by the creditors or where the court has refused to approve a composition, extension of time or scheme of arrangement submitted to it by the official receiver pursuant to a proposal, the court shall endeavour to formulate an acceptable proposal to be submitted to the creditors and the farmer.
May I emphasize the words, "to approve a composition, extension of time or scheme of arrangement". Does that give the powers asked for by the debt conference? They asked that they may have power to (a) alter the terms of the payment of a debt, (b) reduce the principal of the debt and (c) reduce the rate of interest. Does this grant that power?

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS

I have forgotten the words the hon. member read, but that can be done.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:

On section 16-How court to base its proposal.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
This is the only section I can find which sets out any principle to be used as a basis for making this composition by the court. It states:
The court shall base its proposal upon the present and prospective capability of the farmer to meet his debts as they become due and the productive value of the farm.
It will be noted that it is based on two things: first, the ability of the farmer to meet his debt and, second, the productive value of the farm. It seems to me that two vital principles have been left out, principles which ought to guide the court in making this composition. They were both mentioned in the proposed bill submitted to the government. The first was that there should be something there to provide for the preservation of a farmer's equity. The minister made a strong speech this afternoon about retaining confidence. He pointed out that he did not wish to have legislation that was wide open, because creditors would not be prepared to advance money unless they felt they had some security behind the money they advanced. Well, there are two sides to that question. When a creditor lends money to a farmer he is entering into a business partnership. One man

is doing a piece of work with his machinery and his farm; he is putting up the best years of his life. On the other hand, the creditor is putting up some money. If, in the passing years, owing to circumstances beyond the control of both parties, there are no proceeds, what happens? While the equity of the one partner is maintained, the equity of the other partner disappears. If the minister will go over the many cases which can be submitted, he will find that whereas a farmer may have worked for twenty years, may have paid a considerable amount of money in interest, may have put in years of hard work, may have improved his equipment and buildings and increased the number of acres broken, yet at the end of that period his equity has actually shrunk, whereas the equity of the other person is maintained, if not actually increased. The money he invested may have been invested during an inflationary period when the purchasing power of his dollar was much less, and he may be foreclosing at a time of deflation when the purchasing power has greatly increased. The result is that his equity has greatly increased.
It seems to me that one of the weaknesses of this bill is to be found in this section. No provision has been made for attempting to assess the farmer's equity. If these two partners, the creditor and the debtor, are both to suffer a loss on account of bad prices and adverse weather conditions, the loss ought to be shared between them rather than have one party accept all the loss and the other party have all the security. I am in favour of the proposal which was made by the debt conference. They proposed that one of the principles underlying the adjustment of these debts should be:
15. (1) The value of the farmer's interest in the farm lands as represented by the amount of money, principal and interest paid by him to the vendor, mortgagee, encumbrances, or other creditors in respect of the land, and the amount of cultivation, improvements or labour made or expended by him in bringing the lands to their present productive capacity.
I think that ought to be recognized in making the adjustment. The second vital principle which it seems to me has been overlooked was also suggested by the debt conference. It reads:
(3) The cost of maintenance of the debtor and his family at a reasonable standard of living and the current expenditures reasonably necessary in the operation of his farm.
The farmer is not in the same position as a business man. The farm is not only his instrument of production; it is his home. There are cases where a business man may

Farmers' Creditors Act
have his home in his place of business, but that is not the general rule. If, as a result of this business arrangement, he finds at the end of a period of years that the partnership has lost, one partner will get the business, but the other will lose not only the business but his home and the place where his family resides. I think the debt conference made a worth-while suggestion, one worthy of the minister's consideration. They suggest that in any proposal which is made in arranging for the payments to be made by the debtor, sufficient should be left to take care of the farmer and his family. If they cannot stay on the farm as efficient producers; if he cannot maintain his family at a reasonable standard of living, it will be impossible for the farmer to fulfil his part of the obligation.

The court shall base its proposal upon the present and prospective capability of the farmer to meet his debts as they become due and the productive value of the farm.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: It does not guarantee that in the proposal; it does not say that there shall be sufficient allowance for the farmer and his family; that is not considered in the compromise proposal under which the farmer has to pay an amount to the creditor which may make it impossible for him to maintain himself and his family. Under those circumstances the terms of the proposal would be such that he could not fulfil them.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: It would be a very stupid judge who would do that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The suggestion, put forward by my hon. friend attacks the whole basis of fixed money obligations. He has suggested 72537-325}
that a man who is a creditor in a certain amount has an equity in the property. He has not any such thing. He has a claim against the property, which may or may not be secured-if it is in the form of a mortgage it is secured-but he has no opportunity to participate in the increased value of the property. My hon. friend is suggesting that he should participate in the losses. In other words, in the case of a fixed money obligation, the creditor puts up, say, $2,000; the debtor borrows that and the obligation is secured on the real property. Ho puts in a lot of sweat and work over a period of years and for one reason or another the property depreciates in value. The creditor has had no opportunity to participate in any increased value. In other words, my hon. friend has asked that the creditor should transfer to the debtor a portion of the debt. That is what it amounts to. It attacks the whole basis of obligations fixed in terms of money. You may as well say that if a man promises to pay $200 or $300, his legal obligation to pay will depend upon whether or not he is successful in operating a particular property or business in connection with which he has borrowed the money.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: What about his physical obligation? The parliamentary assistant has stated that there is a fixed monetary value.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I did not say anything about fixed monetary value; I said that his obligation was expressed in terms of money.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
That
obligation is fixed under the proposal as a payment of so much a year. He may have to pay $100 a year, which is his fixed money obligation. It is quite true that the creditor may not participate in any increased profits and that the hon. member for Weyburn is expecting him to participate only in the losses, but the minister is not taking into consideration the fact that once the money obligation is fixed and a condition then comes about over which the farmer has absolutely no control, it may be physically impossible, on account of hail or drouth or something else, for him to carry out that obligation. Then his contract is broken and he cannot possibly help that. The proposal cannot be changed; there cannot be any revision of the proposal, because only one can be made.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Read section 29.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
That covers the annulment of a composition, which brings up an entirely different point. I shall have something to say about that when we reach the section. When the court is to base the proposal upon the present and there is to be only
Farmers' Creditors Act

the one proposal allowed, I think the obligation should be elastic enough to overcome a condition for which the farmer may not be responsible.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I think this section is altogether too vague. It has in the past and will no doubt in the future be interpreted in many different ways and may easily destroy the efficiency of the farmer. In the bill presented by the western conference, section 15 reads:
In exercising its jurisdiction and powers to formulate a plan of settlement and without limiting its discretion in any way the board may consider and determine inter alia the following matters. . . .
(2)	The ability of the debtor to pay and to that end to arrange the payments of his creditors in such amounts and at such times as the debtor may reasonably be expected to meet, having regard to his present and prospective capability to perform the terms and conditions of the plan and having regard to the productive capacity of his farm;
(3)	The cost of maintenance of the debtor and his family at a reasonable standard of living and the current expenditures reasonably necessary in the operation of his farm.
In Alberta the importance of this was realized to such an extent that it became the law of the province, and the first charge against a farmer's production was the amount of the crop which was necessary to carry on the farmer's expenses for the current year. If a farmer is not allowed a sufficient amount from the revenue of his farm to meet these expenditures, he cannot carry on efficiently, and once he has gone under this bill his credit is practically destroyed. It surely must be the aim of the government to allow the farmer to carry on efficiently, and yet this clause as it stands may easily be interpreted in such a way as to allow him just enough to pay certain expenses, without taking into full consideration his costs of living for the family. I had a certain experience years ago, and I do not mind mentioning it, back about the years 1933 or 1934, right in the heart of the depression. A collector was trying to collect a certain bill which at the time I could not pay, on account of crop conditions, and he started to lecture me. He said, " The trouble with you British is you are not satisfied to reduce your standard of living. Central Europeans make better farmers than you do; they are willing to reduce their standard of living down to practically nothing." Is that what we want to do in western Canada- put our farmers there on the plane with the peasants of central Europe? That is what will be done by the bill under this clause; not sufficient provision will be made for the farmer to maintain his farm in a decent state and, in addition, pay the expenses of his

family. It is not necessary for me to say that when the collector took that stand we rapidly parted company.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit a question? Who does he think should pay these costs to which he is referring?

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I think the farmer should be allowed to pay these costs out of the revenue of the farm.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: At whose expense?

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: At no expense; at the cost of the farm. The creditor would have to take less for a year; the debt would be postponed. For instance, if a farm is a total loss, you might say, at whose expense? Well, it is at the expense of the farmer, because that amount is not wiped off the debt; it just means the payment he has to make is postponed until the future. It is always at the farmer's expense until he has to default.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
There is a question I should like to ask in connection with this particular section in order to be in a position to discuss intelligently the meaning and effect of the section, which, I may point out, is identical with the words of the present section 12, subsection 8, of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. Under that section there has been a board which writes off the principal and interest in connection with secured and unsecured debts which have come under the jurisdiction of the boards of review. If the information was already given, I confess that I was not present at the time it was given. I should like to have a statement from the minister showing the total amount of the write-off in secured and unsecured debts in each of the years from 1935, when the act came into effect, until the present time, and what is more important, the percentage of reduction in principal and also in interest during those years. This section has been interpreted by the courts of appeal in the various provinces, not directly but indirectly, through appeals which have been made to the several courts of appeals from orders which have been made by boards of review. As I read over this bill as a whole and this section in particular, I think it actually aims at doing what the land court act of Manitoba endeavoured to do, a statute which was passed on April 17, 1939, but did not come into effect on account of the oncoming of the war. The general purpose of this act, as stated in section 133, is:
.	.	. to retain all honest, industrious and
efficient farmers in the use and occupation of their farms as efficient producers and to make such orders that, after allowing for all normal

Farmers' Creditors Act
current expenditure and providing for the maintenance of themselves and their families in a reasonable standard of comfort, such farmers may be reasonably expected to meet their liabilities as they become due, and to protect in so far as possible the rights of mortgagees and vendors of farm lands.
That, 1 submit, is exactly what has been done under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act-I speak now of Saskatchewan during recent years-in its administration. It is impossible for any judge or any board to foresee what the prospective capabilities of a farm may be. Eventualities will arise. I think it was the hon. member for Weyburn who mentioned the possibility of drouth or hail. I bring that up in connection with this item, for the reason that, for some years now, the boards of review have been making orders which provide that in any one year, irrespective of the order that has been made, if climatic conditions or drouth, frost and the like make it impossible for the farmer to make the payments provided for under the order or the proposal, the sheriff of the judicial district in which he resides may make an order the effect of which is that for that year the order made by the board of review need not be lived up to. situation in the western provinces and who is, therefore, in a position to establish jurisprudence fair alike to the farmer and to the creditor, always having in mind that the primary consideration of this legislation must be the keeping of efficient and honest farmers on the farms, farmers who have found, owing to conditions over which they have no control, that at certain times they are unable to meet their debts in full.
I think we should have the regulations, and I mention that at this time. The regulations will be as important as, if not more important than, the wording of the bill, and I should like to see those regulations that are to direct the administration of this bill, to the end that we may see to what extent the court may go and the considerations it shall take under advisement in determining the question as to the present and prospective capability of the farmer to meet his debts as they become due, and the productive value of the farm. They would go a long way toward clarifying what I believe are the doubts of the hon. member for Weyburn and other members who have spoken. subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS

speechtext: Yes, and that answers the argument hon. members to my left are always raising, to the effect that lawyers will act only when they receive payment.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I did not say that.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: That is the suggestion being made all the time.

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: And it is pretty nearly right, too, is it not?

subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: No, it is not pretty nearly right. All I have to say to the hon. member is this, that if any man in this country has a just action or a just cause of defence, there are lawyers in every province who will undertake his case in order to see that justice is done. Let me say that. It is all very well to regard members of the legal profession as the big boys who represent the big corporations. But the record of the legal profession needs no defence by me to-night. What I have said is merely by way of answer to certain statements made from time to time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: The Moose Jaw declaration will have to be revised on that score.

My suggestion is
this: In Manitoba the appeal court for the province sits in Winnipeg; in Saskatchewan it sits in Regina, and in Alberta it sits in Edmonton and Calgary. It might be costly if the appeal judge were to sit at the seat of the appellate court for the province. My suggestion is that provision be made in the regulations from time to time that at stated periods he shall sit at certain judicial centres. There are twenty-one judicial centres in Sas-

katchewan. I do not know the number in Alberta and Manitoba. In this way the farmers would have the opportunity of appearing personally, if it were necessary for them to do so. A farmer could be present without any unnecessary cost, and he would have an opportunity of hearing personally the arguments advanced by the other side. I feel on the other hand, that unless such a system of sittings is established it may very well be that the cost to the farmer will be prohibitive.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CON SOLID ATI ON OF ARRANGEMENT ACT OF 1934 AND AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I had in mind that the judge would travel and sit at the various places in the province. In fact that was one of the reasons why the court of appeal was one judge, ' rather than a full court. It would be expensive if the appeal were to the court of appeal of the province. This was suggested in another place two or three years ago, but I opposed the proposal, and that led to the falling by the wayside of certain legislation. But with one appeal judge I do not see any reason why he should not travel.

understanding I got. I must say that when these statements are not made loud enough we cannot hear them at this end of the chamber. I think a member of parliament has a right to hear what is being said and it should be spoken loudly enough that he could
hear it. I am strongly opposed to introducing more departments until the others have been taken care of. There are matters that could have been discussed all during the year, and we have not had a motion to go into supply so that we could deal with serious problems. I think there ought to be one or two departments left, because there are plenty of other items to be considered.

I agree with what the hon.
member for Lethbridge has said. At this end of the chamber it is most difficult to hear what is going on. However, I was sitting in another seat last evening and heard what was said, and it was as stated by the minister. I think the hon. member for Lethbridge should allow this item to be introduced, but in future I think the chairman or other hon. members at the other end of the chamber should speak more loudly, so that we may not be precluded from hearing what they are saying.
